content: {"metadata":{"type":"page"},"title":"Precision Video Editing","url":"https://www.notion.so/318c370222d5809babf2f69924809487","text":"Here is the result of "view" for the Page with URL https://www.notion.so/318c370222d5809babf2f69924809487 as of 2026-04-01T20:23:02.184Z: {"title":"Precision Video Editing"} **Goal:** Train a video-to-video model that performs high precision video editing. **Pushing the frontier:**** **While competing T2V models have seen rapid advancement, video editing has lagged behind in capabilities. This offers an opportunity to differentiate ourselves if we can achieve this goal. **People: , , + **will likely recruit a researcher (do reach out!). **Compute estimate: **Hard to say at this point but for creating the datasets perhaps up to 10% of the compute used to create our pre-training video datasets. **Cash estimate: **\$100k-\$1M (possibly more if we aggressively invest in data deals). **Output: **Ultimately, a video-editing variant of FLUX.3 or build this into base FLUX.3 --- We can separate video-to-video generation into two different categories: 1. **Video as context** The input video is used to provide subjects, assets, or setting, but the output does not need to preserve the original clip. For example, generating the next scene of a video using the previous scene as context. 2. **Precision video editing** The input video must be preserved exactly except for the requested change, e.g. “add a cowboy hat to the character” or “replace the content of a digital billboard with this video.” **Video as context** is relatively easy given the data we have. **Precision video editing** is more difficult and what we should aim to achieve --- ### Hypothesis & Training Strategy For **video as context**, we can train at scale by splitting videos into sequential pairs: first half as input, second half as output. If captioned well enough, this teaches the model how to extract and reuse visual context, but it does not teach it to preserve the original video. Precision editing requires training pairs where *everything is the same except the intended change*. The ideal data would be Hollywood-grade VFX plates paired with final shots, or multiple takes of the same scene with controlled differences. But this data is hard to acquire at scale (if at all). We faced an similar problem during Flux Kontext development. We had large datasets of image pairs sourced from the same photoshoots that gave general editing capability but poor controllability & precision, because multiple factors changed at once (pose, camera angle, expression). The model learned to general capabilities but not to make constrained, precise changes. We fixed this by adding a much smaller dataset (\~50k samples) focused explicitly on precision edits. I think we can approach video in the same way. A **two-stage approach** 1. **Large-scale mid-training** to learn general video editing priors. 2. **Targeted fine-tuning** to enforce precision, controllability, and preservation. --- ## Stage 1: Large scale mid-training datasets The goal here is to train the model on many forms of “related video pairs”. **1. Within-scene video pairs** Extract multiple clips from the same scene and train on pairs, with instruct captions. - Highly scalable. - Will learn how to use visual context from videos, but a weak signal for precision. - It may be a challenge to identify clips with an interesting relationship between them. **2. Generated video pairs** Edit the first and/or last frame of a video, then use a frame-conditioned video model to generate to generate a very similar video to the original with the edit applied. With strong captioning that details all the differences between the videos I think this will be a much stronger prior for fine-tuning in precision video editing than the within scene video pairs approach. - Scales with budget; estimated cost \~\$0.5–\$1 per sample if we use existing leading video models. Though maybe we could do this ourselves cheaper once the base flux 3 t2v model is finished - Plausible size: \~50k to 1M+ **3. Open-source video editing datasets** In particular: - Senorita-2M (h/t ) **4. Generalizing from image-editing** Strong image-editing abilities will be a very useful prior for learning precision video editing. --- ## Stage 2: Fine-tuning for precision editing This stage explicitly trains the model to preserve everything except the requested edit. **1. Video editing templates (After Effects pipeline)** Automated rendering of After Effects projects with parameterized edits (text editing, input image/video assets, layer addition/removal). - Highly precise. - Covers motion graphics and text-editing use cases. - Plausible scale: 50k–500k video pairs. It is plausible to acquire 100k+ source projects. ```plain text Data Flow S3 Bucket (incoming/*.zip) │ ▼ LISTENER (nexlistener.js) │ 1. Polls S3 for new ZIPs (read-only, never deletes) │ 2. Discovers render nodes via EC2 tags (Role=render-node) │ 3. Health-checks nodes, picks the one with most free capacity │ 4. Downloads ZIP, POSTs it to the best node's /api/v2/batches │ ▼ RENDER NODE (nexserver.js) │ 5. Extracts ZIP, cleans macOS residues │ 6. Runs AfterFX.com headlessly (aeCompose_v3.jsx) to: │ - Relink missing footage │ - Extract project structure (layers, comps, text, fonts) │ 7. Generates nexrender task JSON from the structure │ 8. Forks N+1 children (1 base + N randomized variants) │ - Each child gets its own project dir copy │ - Randomizer modifies text/visibility/opacity/effects/media/color/transform │ 9. Queues children through the render pipeline (aerender → ffmpeg → MP4) │ ▼ LISTENER (polls batch status) │ 10. As each child job finishes, downloads its MP4 + metadata │ 11. Uploads MP4 + metadata to the receiver │ ▼ RECEIVER (nexreceiver.js) 12. Stores MP4s as output/

content: {"metadata":{"type":"page"},"title":"VLM Adaptation for Noisy Latents","url":"https://www.notion.so/313c370222d5818fbdb7cc35a1b3bdaf","text":"Here is the result of "view" for the Page with URL https://www.notion.so/313c370222d5818fbdb7cc35a1b3bdaf as of 2026-03-02T12:58:43.001Z: {"title":"VLM Adaptation for Noisy Latents"} # TL;DR Fine tune a VLM to be able to answer questions about noisy latents. Later use it to do content moderation, quality assessment, training losses etc. # Motivation Vision-Language Models (VLMs) are increasingly valuable tools in our generative modeling pipeline: they can evaluate output quality, flag unsafe content, and serve as reward signals for post-training via RL-based fine-tuning. Work like Dual-Process Image Generation \[1\] and the image editing approach of Kumari et al. \[2\] demonstrate that differentiating VLM feedback directly through the generation process can unlock powerful new training paradigms. However, all of these applications share a fundamental bottleneck: **VLMs were trained on clean, pixel-space images.** As such, using them with our models typically requires many denoising steps followed by decoding the latent through the VAE back into pixel space. This is expensive and limits the contexts in which we can apply VLM reasoning. The ability to query a VLM at arbitrary points in the denoising trajectory (on intermediate noisy latents `z_t` ) is beneficial for three key reasons: - **Differentiable training signals during denoising**: Backpropagating through the full denoising chain is expensive; if a VLM could evaluate intermediate latents, we could obtain richer per-step reward signals without decoding at every timestep. - **Faster quality evaluation and guidance**: During inference, we could apply VLM-based checks or guidance (e.g. for content moderation or composition quality) at intermediate denoising steps rather than only at the end. - **Step-level preference optimization**: Methods like LPO \[3\] and DiNa-LRM \[4\] show that step-level preference modeling over noisy latents is more efficient and avoids domain mismatch from pixel-space rewards — but these currently rely on repurposed diffusion models rather than the semantically richer understanding of VLMs. The bottleneck is that noisy latents look nothing like the clean images VLMs were trained on. At high noise levels, the signal-to-noise ratio is very low, and even decoded noisy images are heavily blurred or structureless. The standard VLM vision encoder, typically a CLIP or SigLIP ViT, simply cannot extract useful features from these inputs. ![](https://prod-files-secure.s3.us-west-2.amazonaws.com/d47c9781-7a36-4f60-98ec-c16fd7b286a6/c4f6d9ab-43c4-401b-9833-50d915a45175/drawio.drawio.png?X-Amz-Algorithm=AWS4-HMAC-SHA256&X-Amz-Content-Sha256=UNSIGNED-PAYLOAD&X-Amz-Credential=ASIAZI2LB466XJDBBXTU%2F20260419%2Fus-west-2%2Fs3%2Faws4_request&X-Amz-Date=20260419T164238Z&X-Amz-Expires=3600&X-Amz-Security-Token=IQoJb3JpZ2luX2VjED8aCXVzLXdlc3QtMiJIMEYCIQD7%2FolV3s1Q5L3deOGQBLZrJjTYFuspnMFUGJf05FzfvAIhAIv0vxuM2A%2BMZ53lBME95kTrU3OwzG1BW%2FeC%2Boxffup9Kv8DCAgQABoMNjM3NDIzMTgzODA1Igyiotg2Nq4mej%2BEmvIq3AN7pIlp42oV7fLJeQEATx%2BJQ7n3GeETq9hA4rz9dPhM9mGXSeMtuVnYMk%2BU4mLiuaQ4KTk8fmSKK2PLvO06LpQDkSy%2B0v9LN5jUDxf9Fdau3BU95VziDft93TZutWBFi11D%2FFF3un1lK%2FBTOuYmQQILc0WeIjTjWs%2FKSDwoE0PIjwU7ho2Oqdxz0IWeMfuPYIbiggIi165RC0SVCdDQQEo6wrAuR66PPP7VKk6F%2B6t%2FERbMmm6z5LgRFnHVNjPX3eS8eDh5Natb9fKNFr5k%2B4AaoZHGqM7tDU%2FUChorjb59hlUkx295Ut1CrwbUSn1R%2F1NtQ1T8DAk4HJUxdt15WdG%2Bp%2FSVKWAP7c%2BjVT0loP%2BF%2BPJUeT5Lr1F%2FrJNYuuDyV1FY8Orb79SgZGEXy2qZSuUM89sEcmOgRtEy1ELpEfv8XXsits5yIGp5aUhm%2Ba%2BuQhNCJGSGWSrFkG3EiTEMpYwBPL6I0fHxRPa9ottoTir8c6Sy6gJlzL1StgjFAD0ZmvIlH9FKkYmg5JEcKAoKG0Nxk5hxUehpvQC1a9IYBB5%2FMMRiNuGiy7m3zUjOgif5OuIyHMPiSs%2Bh96z8ve6gN%2BEzqhEPrqT0ufX21QYeJ%2FXX9f5xIFvhvmNOV0lDtTCv0ZPPBjqkAZ0CU%2B9s0KY2dmatY%2F2Vuye9O84i%2BB9hXbvpvd2eXV2NnkB3Rr9ykBPMEz0Y%2BMBYsMP3DEgcAnsrLwBCE2QMyo43O7VaFlV3fSVpou4rSK6S8JdvzaxArjmi9vtCeu0idy32zKPN0xTsQUlgEZSyJHQv8JmQweIl5dsaWekoABni2msdyXPmJUMeL1XjmwUJVGWp6E8xExgFxQOK5SSD5LFgogmd&X-Amz-Signature=e3c4a004699a30a2989a340bdf5debc5efc25af8315d7992dc7faa458c0be16c&X-Amz-SignedHeaders=host&x-amz-checksum-mode=ENABLED&x-id=GetObject) # Core Idea We propose to **fine-tune a VLM with a new input pathway for noisy diffusion latents**, enabling it to reason about intermediate denoising states as if querying the clean image. Concretely, the approach adds: - A **new projection tower** that maps noisy latent tokens `z_t`, conditioned on the timestep `t`, into the VLM's token embedding space. This replaces the standard ViT vision encoder for the latent input path. - **LoRA adapters** on the VLM's language model backbone, allowing the model's language-space reasoning to adapt to the noisier, semantically compressed representations coming from the latent path. The key insight is that the latent `z_t` already contains structure that correlates with the clean image, and that a learned, timestep-conditioned projection can extract this structure in a form the VLM's LLM backbone can usefully process. Ongoing approaches may consider `z_0` predictions created by a single pass through the network (to avoid having to predict information from high frequency input noise), or the use of internal diffusion features to augment the latent projection tower. ## Training Approaches We will initially consider two complementary training strategies: **Approach A — Supervised VQA on Noisy Latents** The most direct approach: encode the clean image through the VAE to get `z_0`, apply forward diffusion noise to obtain `z_t` at a sampled timestep `t`, then train the VLM with standard instruction-tuning losses (VQA, captioning, etc.) where the ground-truth answers are derived from the **original clean image**. The model learns to answer questions about the clean image's content given only the noisy latent as visual input. ```python # Approach A: VQA-style supervision z_0 = vae_encode(clean_image) # VAE-encode clean image z_t = add_noise(z_0, t) # Apply forward diffusion noise at timestep t tokens = latent_projection_tower(z_t, t) # New timestep-conditioned projection logits = vlm_backbone(tokens, question) # VLM with LoRA adapters loss = cross_entropy(logits, clean_image_answer) # Ground truth from clean image ``` **Approach B — Internal Feature Matching (Representation Distillation)** A complementary approach where rather than relying on language supervision alone, we explicitly align the internal features produced by the latent projection tower with the features the VLM's standard ViT encoder would produce for the corresponding clean image. This can be a cosine similarity loss on the projected token sequences, or a token-level distillation loss. The intuition is to make the noisy latent's representation functionally equivalent to the clean image's visual representation from the VLM's perspective, so that the LLM backbone sees approximately the same input regardless of the denoising stage. ```python # Approach B: Feature matching distillation z_0 = vae_encode(clean_image) z_t = add_noise(z_0, t) # Noisy path (trainable) noisy_tokens = latent_projection_tower(z_t, t) # Clean path (frozen VLM vision encoder) clean_tokens = vlm_vision_encoder(vae_decode(z_0)).detach() # Feature alignment loss loss_align = 1 - cosine_similarity(noisy_tokens, clean_tokens).mean() # Optionally combine with VQA loss loss = loss_vqa + lambda_align * loss_align ``` Intuitively, approach B would likely push the encoding in the roughly correct region of the embedding space, while the VQA-style loss would ensure it does not deviate to out-of-domain regions where the model can no longer be used as a VLM. # Related Work **VLMs as rewards for diffusion training.** Dual-Process Image Generation \[1\] shows that backpropagating VLM logit-level gradients through a frozen image generator enables learning new control tasks from VLM feedback in minutes. Kumari et al. \[2\] train image editing models entirely without paired data by unrolling the diffusion trajectory and using VLM loss as the training signal — they notably observe that multi-step models are necessary because "at the early stages of diffusion, the model has a noisy or blurry estimate of the final output," exactly the domain gap we aim to address. Clark et al. \[5\] showed early on that VLM feedback via DDPO can improve text-image alignment without human labels. **Reward modeling on noisy latents.** LPO / LRM \[3\] proposes to repurpose diffusion model components themselves for step-level preference modeling directly in the latent space, avoiding pixel-space decoding and domain mismatch. DiNa-LRM \[4\] extends this with noise-calibrated Thurstone likelihood and timestep-conditioned scoring, showing that aggregating features across multiple noise levels (noise ensembling) improves robustness. Both works demonstrate the value of operating in the noisy latent domain but use diffusion backbones rather than the richer semantics of VLMs. **VLM architecture: projection towers and adapters.** LLaVA \[6\] and LLaVA-1.5 \[7\] establish the standard paradigm of connecting a frozen vision encoder to a frozen LLM via a learned projection (linear or MLP), with optional LoRA adapters. Our approach will follow this framework but replace the standard ViT encoder with a new learned tower that ingests noisy latents conditioned on timestep. **Fine-tuning CLIP on noisy latents.** Luo et al. \[8\] fine-tune a CLIP encoder to accept noisy diffusion latents as inputs and operate as latent-space evaluators for dynamic CFG scheduling. This is the closest prior work to our core proposal — they demonstrate the feasibility of adapting a vision encoder to process noisy latents at various timesteps — though they focus on lightweight discriminative evaluators rather than the full generative reasoning of a VLM. # Potential Use Cases **Differentiable training signal without full decoding.** If the adapted VLM can evaluate a noisy latent `z_t` without requiring VAE decode, it can be queried at intermediate denoising steps during unrolled diffusion training. This is directly relevant to post-training approaches like those in \[1\] and \[2\], potentially making them cheaper and enabling richer step-level feedback. **Content moderation during generation.** Current content moderation requires waiting for a fully denoised + decoded image. A noisy-latent VLM could flag likely policy violations mid-trajectory, enabling early termination of problematic generations before they complete — a significant efficiency and safety improvement. **Step-level RLHF / GRPO.** With a reward signal that can evaluate arbitrary noisy latents, step-level policy optimization methods (cf. LPO \[3\], CGRU \[9\]) become accessible with VLM-quality semantic understanding rather than diffusion-backbone classifiers. **Quality estimation during generation.** Providing users or downstream systems with quality estimates mid-generation, without requiring the full denoising trajectory to complete. # Downsides & Risks - **Domain gap may be too large at high noise levels.** At `t` close to 1 (pure noise), even a learned projection may not contain recoverable semantic signal. Training may need to focus on lower-to-mid noise levels, potentially limiting usefulness for very early denoising steps. - **Latent space specificity.** The projection tower is trained on FLUX's VAE latent space. Reuse across different VAEs (e.g. for different resolutions or model variants) may require retraining or fine-tuning. # Compute Needs - Training is relatively lightweight compared to full diffusion model training: only the projection tower and LoRA adapters need gradient updates. - However, the VLM backbone itself (even frozen) requires significant VRAM. Inference of a 7B–32B VLM during training limits batch size. - Minimum viable: \~4 nodes (for small VLM + reasonable batch size) - Ideal: \~16 nodes (for larger VLMs or higher batch sizes) # References \[1\] Luo, G. et al. {"metadata":{"type":"page"},"title":"Long Context: RAG + Persistent State","url":"https://www.notion.so/313c370222d580378dd7e9897a86f51c","text":"Here is the result of "view" for the Page with URL https://www.notion.so/313c370222d580378dd7e9897a86f51c as of 2026-04-16T18:43:16.792Z: {"title":"Long Context: RAG + Persistent State"} ## TLDR To act as faithful agents in the real world, visual models need to reason across vast temporal horizons (minutes/ hours, not seconds). Current models hit a **"memory wall"** where they must either crash or compress the past into a lossy, blurry representation. This project proposes an **Autoregressive Retrieval-Augmented Generation (AR-RAG)** framework. By decoupling **Memory Retrieval** from **Frame Synthesis**, we allow the model to autoregressively predict the next frame while maintaining access to a high-fidelity, "infinite" historical index. --- ## The Problem: The Finite Context Bottleneck To be deployed as agents in real-world scenarios (robotics, autonomous driving, or long-form assistant roles) visual models must reason across vast temporal context to ensure logical consistency and "faithfulness" to previous events. ### Status Quo Limitations 1. Directly increasing the input context length makes inference computationally infeasible as context grows with time. 2. Existing solutions rely on aggressive spatial or temporal downsampling. This compromises fine-grained details necessary for faithful generation. > 💬 We need a solution that provides manageable context length per generation without losing or compromising information along the way. ![](https://prod-files-secure.s3.us-west-2.amazonaws.com/d47c9781-7a36-4f60-98ec-c16fd7b286a6/b55b23ed-8566-45b1-b432-95db587ecaa4/image.png?X-Amz-Algorithm=AWS4-HMAC-SHA256&X-Amz-Content-Sha256=UNSIGNED-PAYLOAD&X-Amz-Credential=ASIAZI2LB466UMYV7X3P%2F20260419%2Fus-west-2%2Fs3%2Faws4_request&X-Amz-Date=20260419T164240Z&X-Amz-Expires=3600&X-Amz-Security-Token=IQoJb3JpZ2luX2VjED8aCXVzLXdlc3QtMiJIMEYCIQDy8tyIb1Qp8prLKS6Q89p3WItvUiQNFLs77Q1nL7fqiAIhANpPPmMC%2FPt%2BdTe0jxB2AXV7CzFVSlJkSVTUMqdJNO6XKv8DCAgQABoMNjM3NDIzMTgzODA1IgziS85XVWPGM%2B24AX0q3APwmYbeZrRVkxwEGkV%2Fu9UddQTQ8cETAq1MirkAXxWwUDJVU3waIgV9jC8hlqRTTE9ZhV5X1ZtO9FsK2HTghuNAQ7QOEHbpmBjzs%2BwHBX2sLfh2x7%2ButTwr3K0OSyly2uxqIvlId7uJXT0WrDTJ8iZFjFkcLuNvonwipyJQeVmNPzRk0OI0m629bW1wmZPo27lqBRVdEOG277RoIVDu2jhNASL0XaGti8RKQwRWvGw8fM3mq9RgECiYbhL8HlZpUvhPbLB4jaUv%2FClfWyiiWpYT90jORgaN%2BoBKDvxpqZXhAHgpPa%2BUjIZCWvuAPjcxvFw5Dw%2BQemO0IdekTwFShFeSGWr97d4gRZKwSJOjvyXZz3D0QVDalUm3cpZfZLnhvFD2hYL%2FwLWLs2WweCkIsYgLekNFpxYEP07nAbGc0gkvz%2FPgpDCylcsu5FSyFcP8GKDk0C%2FSftCo2d7HlcI2UaxyeqBMN0M8R80aRFtFlgr7vD2brkWminbweGL6uQLLRcQ1%2BvqYoxpAqPwJ%2FO9XtJvXfLrzTkjszWwQ%2FaA6JFwBqExosWHanSWkFfiZxEJNiOLmGtljmyI1DwVkIVvwS2VtavuSARSFpsGkUvkGB7pcBU%2B92vXVnAYNjve6rTDczpPPBjqkAZfIZinzi92E9H1rTL2ojYM%2Bvm06hKGPAxLSQ3ahGP%2FFlmLjzgka3etp2ldlVN5xEYtZuDt2w0nrGcL%2FmJ8vSoebLbSdIUUT8CCEwrlsqzSE9K%2FcStj9aCumCG%2FQz5zwDQUkkrbXYuYLVwh5T%2FvpiEMINqQqvgsIvvXZeKnEZ%2BXity4TJ9Y0sxBHfPZWgbp6WsUeIcI0QhtgXLODcqucDvrlabvB&X-Amz-Signature=a491e52a9c6d928cb53dc0b05fab9bc0fe0b3b7f820b2d8e71aff0af4be7966d&X-Amz-SignedHeaders=host&x-amz-checksum-mode=ENABLED&x-id=GetObject) **Figure 1:** *Comparison of Approaches. Current models (left) face an overflow (aka “overltipe” since the model is not perfect at typography) of memory or information loss via compression. Our proposal (right) provides a consistent, manageable input to the generator, resulting in higher fidelity over long sequences.* --- ## 💡 The Proposition: Compression- out, focus- in This proposal builds on two key insights: 1. **Information Sparsity-** For a given video frame generation step, the model does not need the full preceding context. It only needs the *relevant* context (e.g., if a character picks up an object they set down 30 minutes ago, the model only needs the context of that original moment, not the intervening 30 minutes). 2. **Self-Supervision for Representation**- Building on our previous work **Self-Flow**, we know that self-supervised objectives learn powerful visual representations which are highly beneficial for generation as well. We propose a framework where the generator operates on a **manageable, concise set of high-fidelity context frames**, intelligently selected from an "infinite" storage vault. --- ## Proposed Architecture: The Retrieve-and-Generate Pipeline We will train two components simultaneously using a **joint self-supervised objective** (predicting the next sequence of frames): ### 1. The Retriever (Encoder) - **Role:** Active memory management - **Mechanism:** Has access to the entire raw historical context (e.g., the past 2 hours of video stored as latent representations) - **Task:** For the current generation timestep t, queries the history and retrieves the top-N most relevant preceding frames (or their high-level features). The retriever will be a fully self-supervised model, allowing it to learn robust, resilient representations for matching. TBD: how are frames compared? model should probably be conditioned on other inputs, not just the current frame. during training- possible inefficiencies when computing representations for the entire context at each step- should probably address in a smart way. ### 2. <content>
# TL;DR
Extend Self-Flow's self-supervised feature alignment across modalities in a multimodal model. Use the cleaner modality as teacher for the noisier modality's features, learning cross-modal representations without external encoders.
# Core Idea
In a multimodal flow matching model that jointly denoises modalities A and B (e.g., video + audio) via shared transformer blocks:
1. **Per-modality timesteps**: Sample $`t_A`$ and $`t_B`$ independently. The cleaner modality becomes the teacher for that step.
2. **Cross-modal alignment**: At intermediate layer \$l\$, align the noisier modality's features to the cleaner modality's EMA features through a projection head + cosine similarity loss.
3. **Complementary to intra-modal Self-Flow**: The total loss is \$mathcal\{L\}*text\{FM\} + lambda*text\{self\}mathcal\{L\}*text\{self-flow\} + lambda*text\{cross\}mathcal\{L\}_text\{cross-flow\}\$.
```python
# Cross-Flow: single training step
t_video, t_audio = torch.rand(1), torch.rand(1)
z_video, z_audio = noise(video, t_video), noise(audio, t_audio)

h_video, h_audio = model(z_video, z_audio, t_video, t_audio)
loss_fm = flow_loss(h_video, video, t_video) + flow_loss(h_audio, audio, t_audio)

# Cross-modal alignment: cleaner modality teaches noisier one
h_v_l, h_a_l = extract_layer(h_video, L), extract_layer(h_audio, L)
if t_video > t_audio:  # audio is cleaner
    loss_cross = -cos_sim(proj_v(h_v_l), ema(h_a_l))
else:
    loss_cross = -cos_sim(proj_a(h_a_l), ema(h_v_l))

loss = loss_fm + λ_self * loss_self_flow + λ_cross * loss_cross
```
# Why Not Just Self-Flow on a Long Multimodal Sequence?
The obvious baseline is: concatenate tokens from all modalities into one sequence, apply standard Self-Flow (per-token dual-timestep scheduling), and let attention do the rest. Tokens from modality A at low noise will attend to tokens from modality B at high noise, and vice versa — so there's *some* cross-modal information exchange for free.
But this is indirect and incidental. Self-Flow's alignment loss is per-token — it aligns a student layer's features to the EMA teacher layer's features *for the same token*. In a naïve multimodal concatenation:
- A video token's Self-Flow loss aligns its own noisy features to its own clean EMA features. It never explicitly asks "do my features agree with what the audio tokens say about this scene?"
- Cross-modal information only flows through attention, which the model must learn to route correctly on its own. There's no explicit gradient signal pushing cross-modal feature alignment.
- The noise schedule is per-token and modality-agnostic — there's no structure exploiting the fact that modalities carry *complementary* information at different noise levels.
Cross-Flow adds the explicit cross-modal alignment loss: align the noisier modality's intermediate features to the cleaner modality's features (via EMA / stop-gradient). This directly incentivizes shared semantic representations across modalities, rather than hoping attention learns this implicitly.
# Handling the Token Correspondence Problem
Self-Flow's intra-modal loss has a natural 1:1 token map: token \$i\$'s student features align to token \$i\$'s EMA teacher features. Across modalities, there's no such correspondence — video might have 1024 patch tokens while audio has 128 mel-spectrogram tokens, with entirely different spatial/temporal structure.
Several approaches, in order of simplicity:
- **Global pooling**: Pool each modality's features at layer $`l`$ to a single vector, then align the pooled representations. Simplest, but discards all spatial/temporal structure. Likely a reasonable starting point.
- **Cross-attention pooling**: Use a small cross-attention module where one modality's features query the other's, producing a fixed-size aligned representation. This lets the model learn *which* tokens are semantically relevant across modalities. Modest additional parameters.
- **Temporal alignment (for video+audio)**: If both modalities have a temporal axis, chunk tokens by time window and pool within each chunk, creating a sequence of temporally aligned summary vectors. This preserves coarse temporal structure while handling different token counts per time step.
# Potential Benefits
- **Better cross-modal coherence** in generated outputs (e.g., audio that matches the visual content).
- **Faster convergence for weaker modalities** via cross-modal supervision from the stronger one.
- **Cross-modal representations without external encoders** — features are naturally grounded across modalities.
# Downsides & Risks
- Requires genuinely coupled modalities; harmful for weakly paired data.
- Hyperparameter surface: noise gap, alignment layer, \$lambda_text\{cross\}\$.
- Modest compute overhead from projection heads + EMA features.

title: Adaptive Memory / Streaming
content:
{"metadata":{"type":"page"},"title":"Adaptive Memory / Streaming","url":"https://www.notion.so/318c370222d580deadddfb597eb422c8","text":"Here is the result of "view" for the Page with URL https://www.notion.so/318c370222d580deadddfb597eb422c8 as of 2026-04-19T16:36:16.617Z: {"title":"Adaptive Memory / Streaming"} ## Assets - 03/25/26 overview presentation - [video comparison ](https://285725804eff9c63d0.gradio.live/) ## Scope Make long-term memory banks work effectively in streaming AR video generation — improving quality and consistency for multi-prompt interactive use cases while enabling adaptive serving under runtime constraints. Current systems either lack memory (LongLive) or add memory that helps coarse consistency but compounds errors (MemFlow). We identify root causes through systematic evaluation and visual failure analysis, explore memory designs that address them, and plan adaptive serving that trades memory budget for latency without retraining. **Deliverables:** an evaluation pipeline for multi-prompt interactive video, a post-training recipe that measurably improves cross-segment consistency, and a serving system with a characterized quality–cost Pareto frontier. --- ## Motivation and Impact **Streaming AR video scales length but not memory.**
LongLive (ICLR 2026) combines streaming long tuning with a local attention window (9 latent frames) and a fixed frame sink (3 frames), enabling minute-scale generation at \~20 FPS. But mid-video content becomes inaccessible once it scrolls out of the 12-frame window. Characters introduced later, objects established mid-video, or callbacks to earlier events cannot be recovered. Existing benchmarks like VBench-Long emphasize perceptual quality and short-range consistency and do not directly expose these multi-prompt consistency failures. **Memory banks exist but are double-edged.**
MemFlow (Kling AI, 2025) adds a KV memory bank with text-conditioned saliency (NAM) for what to store. Our evaluation on 100 multi-prompt benchmarks with 10 metrics reveals: MemFlow's bank helps within-segment stability (fewer redundant objects, +6% object count accuracy) but does not improve cross-segment consistency — face identity, transition smoothness, and regional consistency are all tied with LongLive. Visual inspection reveals complementary failure modes: - **LongLive** fails by **forgetting** (identity drift, redundant subjects) - **MemFlow** fails by **remembering wrong things** (phantom objects, identity bleeding at transitions, error compounding) MemFlow's SMA routing, implemented but disabled in their release, actually hurts when enabled. **Memory is also optimized for one narrow operating point.**
MemFlow trains and evaluates around a specific memory configuration. It does not train for serving-time policy variation — changing retrieval budget, compression, or per-layer allocation — making it unclear whether one model can smoothly trade memory budget for latency without quality cliffs. Because NAM's memory construction is text-conditioned, it also misses prompt-agnostic recall: visually salient entities that later reappear without being mentioned in text. **Context Forcing takes a complementary approach**
— training a long-context teacher (20s+) that provides consistency-aware supervision, plus a student-side memory (surprisal-based keyframe selection). Strong results on single-prompt videos (+2.6 subject consistency) but never tested on multi-prompt interactive generation. Their teacher-side fix is composable with our student-side memory design. **No method addresses all failure modes of multi-prompt interactive video generation.**
The field needs better evaluation (metrics that capture multi-prompt consistency), better memory design (store the right content, retrieve it when relevant, prevent error propagation), and adaptive serving (trade memory for latency at runtime). --- ## Approach ### Phase 1 — Evaluation and Failure Analysis ✅ COMPLETE Built a 10-metric evaluation pipeline for multi-prompt interactive video, replacing frame-0-referenced metrics that penalize prompt-following with within-segment variants. **Intra-segment metrics:** image quality, aesthetics, semantic/color stability, prompt adherence
**Inter-segment metrics:** transition smoothness, face identity (ArcFace), regional consistency (DINOv2 patches), object count accuracy (OWLv2), redundancy rate Systematically evaluated LongLive, MemFlow, and MemFlow+SMA on 100 benchmarks. Visual failure analysis documented complementary failure modes. Profiled MemFlow attention: bank gets 9% mass, model largely ignores it. **Key findings:** - MemFlow helps within-segment but not cross-segment (the harder problem) - MemFlow's SMA hurts when enabled — disabled in release for good reason - Bank helps during training at 3000 steps (bank=3 outperforms bank=0) - Three root causes: wrong content stored, can't adapt to new prompts, errors compound ### Phase 2 — Memory Bank Design ✅ COMPLETE Explored memory designs addressing the three root causes. All experiments: 3000 steps, LoRA rank=256, bank_size=3, train-test aligned. Four components: 1. **Keyframe selection** — when bank overflows, cluster by visual similarity, keep one per cluster. Prevents redundancy. 2. **Visual routing** — score bank chunks by latent-space similarity to current generation, attend selectively. Hurts alone (16-d features too coarse) but helps in combination. 3. **Soft transition** — reduce bank influence at prompt switches via ramp. Lets new prompts take effect. 4. **Quality gate** — skip storing corrupted frames. Prevents error compounding. 8 experiments testing components individually and combined. Full combination (all 4) wins 6/10 metrics, beating both baselines: - Face identity: **+0.030** - Regional consistency: **+0.028** - Within-segment semantic: **+0.015** - Transition smoothness: **+0.008** Components are synergistic — none sufficient alone. Keyframe selection is the strongest single lever. **Open questions:** visual inspection favors keyframe-only over full method on some prompts — metrics vs visual quality gap needs per-prompt analysis. Routing contribution unclear without ablation. ### Phase 3 — Ablation and Deeper Understanding 🔜 NEXT 1. **Ablations of full method** — remove one component at a time to quantify individual contributions and determine which are essential. 2. **Per-prompt analysis** — identify which prompts benefit, reconcile aggregate metrics with visual quality. 3. **Richer visual features** — V-JEPA 2 (video-native) or DINO features for routing, replacing 16-d latent means. 4. **Surprisal-based selection** — Context Forcing's continuous, reactive keyframe selection (promote frame when it differs from predecessor) may complement our retroactive deduplication. 5. **Context Forcing combination** — their long-context teacher + our memory design. Complementary: better training signal + better memory management. ### Phase 4 — Memory-Policy Randomization and Tiered Memory 🔮 FUTURE Train with randomized memory policies so one model serves across a range of budgets without retraining: - **Policy randomization:** each training step samples retrieval K, depth, compression tier, per-layer budgets. The model learns to use memory robustly across a family of configurations rather than one fixed regime. - **Tiered memory:** stage complexity — pooled summary tokens (always-on baseline), add visually salient tokens (attention heavy-hitters), add novelty bursts (scene changes). Each tier independently justified. - **Visual/latent-driven construction:** decide what enters the bank based on latent signals (not just text similarity), enabling prompt-agnostic recall of mid-video content. ### Phase 5 — Adaptive Serving 🔮 FUTURE Because the model would be trained with policy randomization (Phase 4), the serving system can trade memory budget vs latency without retraining: - On-device retrieval — bank stays on GPU, no CPU round-trips - Combined local + memory attention in single pass per layer - Mask reuse across denoising steps within a chunk - Quantized memory (FP8/INT8) for deeper history at matched budgets - Per-layer budgets — more memory for semantic layers, less for texture layers - Content-aware eviction — keep frequently-retrieved entries, drop stale ones - Beyond-training-horizon serving (120s, 300s from 60s training) ### Phase 6 — Scaling and Paper 🔮 FUTURE Prototype on Wan2.1-T2V-1.3B (current). Scale to larger models for final results. Primary comparisons vs LongLive, MemFlow, and Context Forcing on multi-prompt interactive benchmarks. --- ## Current Status
Phase Status
Phase 1: Evaluation + failure analysis ✅ Complete — 10 metrics, 100 prompts, visual failure analysis
Phase 2: Memory bank design ✅ Complete — 8 experiments, full method wins 6/10 metrics
Phase 3: Ablation + understanding 🔜 Next — planned
Phase 4: Policy randomization 🔮 Future
Phase 5: Adaptive serving 🔮 Future
Phase 6: Scaling 🔮 Future
--- ## Existing Work
Method Memory Result Relationship
LongLive (ICLR 2026) Fixed sink + local window (12 total frames) SOTA real-time interactive video (20.7 FPS) Our foundation
MemFlow (Kling AI, 2025) KV bank (text-selected, SMA disabled in release) Helps within-segment, not cross-segment Baseline — text-based, no error prevention
Context Forcing (2026) Surprisal Slow-Fast Memory + long-context teacher +2.6 subject consistency (single-prompt only) Complementary — teacher-side, composable
VideoSSM Evolving SSM state Alternative memory mechanism Alternative approach
PaFu-KV Learned salience from bidirectional teacher Future-aware KV eviction Inspiration for learned selection
Helios Multi-resolution memory patchification 14B real-time Inspiration for tiered memory
--- ## Risks and Mitigations **Aggregate metrics vs visual quality gap**
Full method wins on metrics but visual inspection doesn't always confirm.
→ Mitigation: per-prompt analysis and ablation study (Phase 3). **Routing contribution unclear**
Hurts alone, unclear if it helps in combination or other components carry the full method.
→ Mitigation: ablation (Phase 3). **Policy randomization may not help**
If the model doesn't learn to adapt across budgets.
→ Mitigation: start with fixed best config, add randomization incrementally (Phase 4). **Serving overhead too high**
Memory adds latency.
→ Mitigation: mask reuse, quantization, per-layer budgets (Phase 5). **Memory value saturates**
If the bank concept is fundamentally limited for streaming video.
→ Mitigation: Context Forcing combination (teacher-side fix), alternative mechanisms (SSM, reference conditioning). --- ## Key References - [LongLive](https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.22622) — Streaming long tuning with frame sink (Yang et al., ICLR 2026) - [MemFlow](https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.14699) — Narrative adaptive memory for streaming video (Kling AI, 2025) - [Context Forcing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.06028) — Long-context teacher + Slow-Fast Memory (Chen et al., 2026) - [VideoSSM](https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.04519) — SSM-compressed global memory for AR video - [PaFu-KV](https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.21896) — Past- and future-informed KV cache salience (Chen et al., 2026) - [Helios](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.04379) — 14B real-time long video generation (Yuan et al., 2026) - [VBench-Long](https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.13503) — Video generation evaluation Adaptive Memory for Streaming Auto Regressive Video v0 "}

content:
{"metadata":{"type":"page"},"title":"VAE/SSL Pre-training","url":"https://www.notion.so/317c370222d5805fbac6fb1734902f80","text":"Here is the result of "view" for the Page with URL https://www.notion.so/317c370222d5805fbac6fb1734902f80 as of 2026-04-19T16:34:27.941Z: {"title":"VAE/SSL Pre-training"} # VAE+SSL Joint Pre-training for Video ## Research Question / Hypothesis Can we make video VAE latents more learnable by jointly training with SSL objectives (DINO, [V-JEPA](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.08471)) — while keeping reconstruction quality intact? And if the learned representations are strong enough, can the encoder double as a foundation for downstream conditioning and planning? The core idea: reconstruction-only VAE training produces latents biased toward low-level pixel info. More training compute → better reconstruction but generation quality stagnates or gets worse. [VTP](https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.13687) showed this clearly for images (see Fig 1 below). Adding understanding objectives (CLIP, SSL) fixes this — generation improves with compute. We want to do this for video, where temporal semantics matter and image-based SSL (like what [REPA-E](https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.10483) uses) isn't enough. **Hypotheses:** - Joint VAE+SSL training injects semantic structure into latents → better learnability for downstream diffusion - V-JEPA style objectives may be better than DINO for video since they capture motion/temporal stuff. V-JEPA 2 hits 77.3% on SSv2 with a frozen encoder + attentive probe — that's pure motion understanding from SSL alone, no labels during pre-training. More importantly, it shows these representations transfer to planning: the same encoder enables zero-shot robot control after minimal post-training. This is the kind of latent structure we want in our VAE — if SSL quality is high enough, the encoder becomes reusable for downstream conditioning and planning, not just tokenization. - This should scale — more VAE pre-training compute should keep helping generation (unlike rec-only which plateaus) ### Core figure from [VTP](https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.13687) (Yao et al., 2025) ![](https://prod-files-secure.s3.us-west-2.amazonaws.com/d47c9781-7a36-4f60-98ec-c16fd7b286a6/49acc9e0-3573-480b-8010-4e8081940b67/Screenshot_2026-03-02_at_9.54.07_PM.png?X-Amz-Algorithm=AWS4-HMAC-SHA256&X-Amz-Content-Sha256=UNSIGNED-PAYLOAD&X-Amz-Credential=ASIAZI2LB466Z6O3FYQE%2F20260419%2Fus-west-2%2Fs3%2Faws4_request&X-Amz-Date=20260419T164248Z&X-Amz-Expires=3600&X-Amz-Security-Token=IQoJb3JpZ2luX2VjED8aCXVzLXdlc3QtMiJGMEQCIByKboQOdfN%2BPDQyFG2rSXmmr%2FuR0pFgLOuQne7cmiiWAiBfd6Mw40z%2BlGhfV3dKZLrMDA8MhTvgu7QBdizTfXo5cyr%2FAwgIEAAaDDYzNzQyMzE4MzgwNSIM%2BMpeZyo5MSGs3xG7KtwD8NCEm%2Fk6euoquJEBMel1%2BwTSDAn2rXPeqF1%2BIGycuHEAim0OXbRFadrWJbuyCkKfS32J7Fn37hUrfM4TgFqDwMujqsSGnesMLzusuIbACLmMJ68DXq%2BKXtsf%2Bx06H4LZEZMuNVSi%2B4lX96KkxkHNSbwxOHS8yAIiGF2PHwGM7%2Fh8qjAOmKhfc67mUAUOGavh4OoSSu5s4qhDyKaYgpgaO74xPap7p8EO%2BkDJ67W1XuWnXL27Bqmyal5LTTsWZ5LrTitaAClr%2BcvrjASfUrUcpVQ408opCdB7LLfhQmjC49QcY31EuMXOP2IrAXv99yKKLsp0sUdk9g7T9Uk7XKBoTFgDduewaatQqzM5GcTJmTplyGWYHy0s6%2FEKbDGB43G0%2BE99MOj6aFPRDAasxWIGy2LapmgYZdSnTYjUWktWSbOdII7pgeu3IexDaflmycuXYN%2BHCc2Z4%2Fxf961ERzxOe5xWIecmnfAmLEUw%2FCPBVJEFgu6jKUHpIsHKG0%2BQwriLY%2Bvzs333QoyKLsczIlc7qrNoyClIA5GAigEJF%2B4BtwXVoH6nWGj6stpVfpyKluJvBaPQ%2F5%2BkMzJEzpWH2i9sFpTBz7yvtkHYhqsQIk6iUMPZb9rRjqKkliXm1wIwmc2TzwY6pgHZkccQ9K%2BvRSYEuc43KkZGjabaf2DHki3Qu92MtdbZswypw91TDHXfqepC1FzBGClmNRDErEcfyHTtyRkM5NSQE%2FixgrPt35JiyMOUMDPV0KIRFIK90V7ti%2FDdYnbpsWUZMH66GXQWu3cwNWJYEQ5RrT11q9l6gHUNAnAlI8nxBG7j4fYav1%2FvdTee1QADNEyKcQPABl5DBeD1cQGNrwLkwQP%2BeJJA&X-Amz-Signature=9e34b54cf8baa55f44da7f31dcea1d00b355705c863fdbda914acf67c9f5524d&X-Amz-SignedHeaders=host&x-amz-checksum-mode=ENABLED&x-id=GetObject) *Fig 1: From VTP paper. SSL+AE and CLIP+AE show correlated growth in generation and understanding with compute. Reconstruction-only AE stagnates. We want to replicate this behavior for video with video-native SSL.* ## Why this matters Current approaches each have clear problems (see also [BFL's representation comparison](https://bfl.ai/research/representation-comparison) and [Sander Dieleman's latent space post](https://sander.ai/2025/04/15/latents.html) for broader context on the learnability-reconstruction trade-off): - [**RAE**](https://rae-dit.github.io/) (frozen DINOv2 + trained decoder): Good learnability but reconstruction is bad — color shifts, texture errors. Frozen image encoder, no temporal understanding for video. - [**REPA-E**](https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.10483) (end-to-end VAE+diffusion via REPA loss): Strong image results but ties VAE optimization to diffusion training. Uses DINOv2 which is image-only — not ideal for video. - [**VTP**](https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.13687) (CLIP+SSL+rec for images): Proves the scaling thesis but image-only, hasn't been extended to video. Our angle: **video-native SSL directly in VAE pre-training, decoupled from diffusion**. This gives us: - Reusable tokenizer (not entangled with diffusion like REPA-E) - Trainable encoder with reconstruction loss (not frozen like RAE) - Temporal understanding from [V-JEPA](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.08471) / [V-JEPA 2](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.09985) - Potential encoder reuse for conditioning and planning — if probe accuracy is high enough, the encoder has generic video understanding and can serve as a conditioning backbone. V-JEPA 2 demonstrates this concretely: their self-supervised video encoder, after post-training with just 62 hours of unlabeled robot data, enables zero-shot robotic planning via model predictive control in latent space — picking and placing objects in unseen environments without any task-specific training or reward. If our VAE encoder internalizes similar temporal-semantic structure through the JEPA objective, it could serve not just as a tokenizer but as the backbone of a world model for planning and action-conditioned generation. The learned latent space could also be used to train a separate V-JEPA-style planning model on top — predicting future latent states conditioned on actions, without needing to retrain the encoder. ## Early Experiment ![](https://prod-files-secure.s3.us-west-2.amazonaws.com/d47c9781-7a36-4f60-98ec-c16fd7b286a6/20aa04cd-1338-4032-bfd6-2a9aefce7c58/Screenshot_2026-03-02_at_10.00.46_PM.png?X-Amz-Algorithm=AWS4-HMAC-SHA256&X-Amz-Content-Sha256=UNSIGNED-PAYLOAD&X-Amz-Credential=ASIAZI2LB466Z6O3FYQE%2F20260419%2Fus-west-2%2Fs3%2Faws4_request&X-Amz-Date=20260419T164248Z&X-Amz-Expires=3600&X-Amz-Security-Token=IQoJb3JpZ2luX2VjED8aCXVzLXdlc3QtMiJGMEQCIByKboQOdfN%2BPDQyFG2rSXmmr%2FuR0pFgLOuQne7cmiiWAiBfd6Mw40z%2BlGhfV3dKZLrMDA8MhTvgu7QBdizTfXo5cyr%2FAwgIEAAaDDYzNzQyMzE4MzgwNSIM%2BMpeZyo5MSGs3xG7KtwD8NCEm%2Fk6euoquJEBMel1%2BwTSDAn2rXPeqF1%2BIGycuHEAim0OXbRFadrWJbuyCkKfS32J7Fn37hUrfM4TgFqDwMujqsSGnesMLzusuIbACLmMJ68DXq%2BKXtsf%2Bx06H4LZEZMuNVSi%2B4lX96KkxkHNSbwxOHS8yAIiGF2PHwGM7%2Fh8qjAOmKhfc67mUAUOGavh4OoSSu5s4qhDyKaYgpgaO74xPap7p8EO%2BkDJ67W1XuWnXL27Bqmyal5LTTsWZ5LrTitaAClr%2BcvrjASfUrUcpVQ408opCdB7LLfhQmjC49QcY31EuMXOP2IrAXv99yKKLsp0sUdk9g7T9Uk7XKBoTFgDduewaatQqzM5GcTJmTplyGWYHy0s6%2FEKbDGB43G0%2BE99MOj6aFPRDAasxWIGy2LapmgYZdSnTYjUWktWSbOdII7pgeu3IexDaflmycuXYN%2BHCc2Z4%2Fxf961ERzxOe5xWIecmnfAmLEUw%2FCPBVJEFgu6jKUHpIsHKG0%2BQwriLY%2Bvzs333QoyKLsczIlc7qrNoyClIA5GAigEJF%2B4BtwXVoH6nWGj6stpVfpyKluJvBaPQ%2F5%2BkMzJEzpWH2i9sFpTBz7yvtkHYhqsQIk6iUMPZb9rRjqKkliXm1wIwmc2TzwY6pgHZkccQ9K%2BvRSYEuc43KkZGjabaf2DHki3Qu92MtdbZswypw91TDHXfqepC1FzBGClmNRDErEcfyHTtyRkM5NSQE%2FixgrPt35JiyMOUMDPV0KIRFIK90V7ti%2FDdYnbpsWUZMH66GXQWu3cwNWJYEQ5RrT11q9l6gHUNAnAlI8nxBG7j4fYav1%2FvdTee1QADNEyKcQPABl5DBeD1cQGNrwLkwQP%2BeJJA&X-Amz-Signature=7a36f7772474748e68ada7611254027f0dc5f9563f274bf98b9159f9ae12a33f&X-Amz-SignedHeaders=host&x-amz-checksum-mode=ENABLED&x-id=GetObject) *Fig 2: Our preliminary results. Attentive probe on SSv2 motion classification. DINO-style SSL gives \~7% improvement over baseline, and SSL accuracy is still going up at 150k steps while no-SSL has plateaued.* **Original Video** **No SSL** **SSL (DINO)** *PCA visualization of first 3 latents channels. The SSL latents look smoother and detailed than no SSL.* This already shows the encoder is picking up temporal-semantic structure from SSL. ## How we measure success - **rFID / rPSNR**: reconstruction shouldn't degrade much (≤10% vs rec-only baseline) - **Linear/attentive probe accuracy** (SSv2, Kinetics): semantic quality of latent space, should see clear gains - **gFID at fixed DiT budget**: does better latent → better generation? This is the key metric - **Convergence speed**: expect ≥2× faster downstream convergence vs rec-only VAE - **Scaling curve** (gFID vs VAE pre-training FLOPs): should be monotonically improving, not stagnating ## Expected artifacts - Pre-trained video tokenizer checkpoints at multiple scales - Training code + eval pipeline - Video SSL / V-JEPA training and evaluation setup (probe training, SSv2/Kinetics benchmarks) — reusable for future video SSL work and planning model development - Ablation data (SSL variants, loss weights, latent dims, scaling curves) ## Plan **Phase 1 — Exploration** - V-JEPA baseline with ViT is already running — SSv2 attentive probe accuracy (single temporal segment, 1 spatial view) at 300k steps: 43.9%. Still climbing.
Steps 50k 100k 150k 200k 250k 300k
**Accuracy** 39.9% 42.8% 42.0% 42.5% 43.8% 43.9%
- Next: match this with our Swin encoder — Swin's windowed attention is much more efficient to scale to high-res, long videos compared to ViT's quadratic global attention. Our Swin-base (slightly larger than ViT-base) with 2x temporal downsampling and 16x spatial (same as V-JEPA, which does it at patching) is already close early on:
Steps 20k 50k
**Swin (2x temporal, 16x spatial)** 35.2% 41.3%
- Then combine Swin V-JEPA with the VAE reconstruction objective — this is the core experiment - Sweep loss weights (λ_rec, λ_ssl) and batch sampling - Compare against E2E (REPA-E style end-to-end VAE+diffusion training) baseline - Establish scaling curves for each variant - Decision point: does the joint objective beat reconstruction-only at both probe accuracy and downstream generation? **Phase 2 — Scale-up** - Train final tokenizer at scale (Swin-L/XL encoder, large video dataset) - Full downstream diffusion eval - Test encoder reuse for conditioning ## Key References - [VTP: Towards Scalable Pre-training of Visual Tokenizers for Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.13687) — Yao et al., 2025 - [REPA-E: Unlocking VAE for End-to-End Tuning with Latent Diffusion Transformers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.10483) — Leng et al., 2025 - [RAE: Diffusion Transformers with Representation Autoencoders](https://rae-dit.github.io/) — Zheng et al., 2025 - [FLUX.2 VAE: Representation Comparison](https://bfl.ai/research/representation-comparison) — BFL blog, Nov 2025 - [Generative modelling in latent space](https://sander.ai/2025/04/15/latents.html) — Sander Dieleman, Apr 2025 - [V-JEPA](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.08471) — Bardes et al., 2024 - [V-JEPA 2: Understanding, Prediction and Planning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.09985) — Assran et al., 2025 Status Update — April 17, 2026 "}

### Cross-attention pattern for prediction tokens Above we see the cross attention pattern of the query tokens from the noisy prediction frames ( blue) and the keys/values from the clean context tokens (dark green) and the noisy prediction tokens( light green).
For streaming inference we can just use vanilla cudnn sdpa with k,v cache.
Question can this cross attention pattern be implemented efficiently for training:
→ Answer: Yes with only 10% FLOP penalty compared to fastest cudnn sdpa kernel. # **Problem 2: Long context compute** Attention grows quadratically O(N²) making long context expensive during training and inference. **Strategy: ** limit sequence length of context - **Strategy 2.1** More **token efficient context embedding** by using a different encoder for context - **Strategy 2.2 sparse attention** Its easier to understand, the proposed strategies in the context of **teacher forcing, **although they can also be implemented with multi frame diffusion with bi-directional attention. # Strategy 2.1 ** efficient context tokenization** Since we can encode the clean context with a separate network we can choose to encode it in a different embedding space, arguably this context embedding space can: - be higher dimensional (since we don’t need to model it with the generative model) - have higher compression since it should only contain information that is usefull for prediction the future, and does not need to allow for reconstruction. both factors make it likely that if we model a prediction frame with k tokens, we can encode a context with frame with n/k tokens for some k \>\> 1 without loosing quality. See: [The First Fully General Computer Action Model](https://si.inc/posts/fdm1/) This allows us to limit the quadratic growth of the attention to O(N²/2k) + O(N) (see below). If this approach works for high k e.g. k=16, this would speed up long context training and inference (i.e. scenarios bottlenecked by attention) by a factor of 16. We could also modify this setting slightly to train on ultra long context, by choosing different video lengths for the context and the prediction targets, this would only change compute moderately, i.e. for k=16 we could predict 5s clips and condition on 40s context making training only 1.5-2.25 x slower (depending on whether MLPs or attention dominate). Ultra long context understanding could be crucial for visual intelligence. Therefore it might be important to train this at large scale during pretraining vs. tuning this in at postraining. # TL;DR
Give flux reasoning tokens in the style of Tiny Recursive Models ([https://arxiv.org/pdf/2510.04871](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2510.04871)). 
Already shows improved stratified losses vs parameter matched baselines.

# Motivation
The iterative reasoning approach (or inference-time-scaling) has led to major strides in quality in LLMs and reasoning benchmarks like ARC-AGI. A core property of reasoning-based approaches is allowing the model to re-iterate and refine its own predictions using a scratchpad that is not part of the final answer.
We can see different instantiations of this shared idea in prior works:
- **Reasoning in LLMs**: Chain-of-thought (Wei et al., 2022 \[1\]) and scratchpad-based approaches let models iteratively refine their output without increasing model size. This idea has been scaled further in models like OpenAI o1 \[2\] and DeepSeek-R1 \[3\], where extended reasoning chains at inference time yield large gains on hard benchmarks.
- **Reasoning in small models (HRM, TRM)**: HRM \[4\] and TRM \[5\] demonstrate that a small model iterated many times can match the performance of much larger models. TRM, a 2-layer, 7M-parameter network with recursive forward passes, achieves 40% on ARC-AGI-1, competitive with models orders of magnitude larger (e.g., Gemini 2.5 Pro Thinking with 41.0%, Claude Opus 4 Thinking w/ 35.7%).
So far, reasoning approaches in diffusion models have largely explored:
- **LLM-based prompt reasoning**: Using LLMs to reason about a prompt before generation, e.g. to produce intermediate layout representations (bounding boxes, scene graphs) that condition a diffusion model. Representative work: LLM-grounded Diffusion (Lian et al., 2023 \[6\]).
- **Agentic iterative editing**: Using a vision-language model as an agent that generates an image, evaluates it, and iteratively applies edits via tool use. Representative work: Idea2Img (Yang et al., 2023 \[7\]), which uses GPT-4V in a self-refinement loop over a T2I model.
However, we believe a more fundamental reasoning scratchpad-based approach, integrated into the diffusion process itself, can help diffusion models at a deeper level. As one core example, while diffusion models are iterative by nature, key structural decisions (global layout, composition) are made in early denoising steps and are hard to revise. Reasoning tokens embedded in the model itself could give it a mechanism to correct these early-step decisions *within* a single forward pass cycle, rather than from the outside via agent loops.
# Core Idea
**TRM: iterating a small model to match larger ones**
The Tiny Recursive Model (TRM) transforms a standard single-pass model `f(x)` into a recurrent one `f(x, a, r)`, where `x` is the input query, `a` is the most up-to-date answer (initialized to a learned value), and `r` is a set of reasoning tokens (a learned scratchpad). The model iterates, updating `r` and `a` before committing to a final answer:

		```python
# TRM forward pass
a = init_answer()
r = init_reasoning_tokens()

# All but the last answer update cycle: no gradients
with torch.no_grad():
    for _ in range(Y - 1):       # early answer update steps
        for _ in range(X):       # reasoning steps
            r = f(x, a, r).reasoning
        a = f(x, a, r).answer

# Final answer update cycle: backprop through reasoning + answer pass
for _ in range(X):               # reasoning steps (with gradient)
    r = f(x, a, r).reasoning
a = f(x, a, r).answer

# Loss on final answer
loss = criterion(a, target)
		```

**Applying TRM-style reasoning to diffusion**
We map this idea onto a diffusion denoising step. A standard step computes a v-prediction as `v = f(z_t, c, t)`, where `z_t` is the noisy latent, `c` is the text condition, and `t` is the timestep. We extend this to `f(z_t, c, t, v, r)`, where `v` is the current best v-prediction (the "answer") and `r` is a set of reasoning tokens (the scratchpad):
```python
# Reasoning Diffusion forward pass for one denoising timestep
v = init_v_prediction()
r = init_reasoning_tokens()

# All but the last answer update cycle: no gradients
with torch.no_grad():
    for _ in range(Y - 1):       # early answer update steps
        for _ in range(X):
            r = f(z_t, c, t, v, r).reasoning
        v = f(z_t, c, t, v, r).v_prediction

# Final answer update cycle: backprop through all X reasoning steps + answer pass
for _ in range(X):               # reasoning steps (with gradient)
    r = f(z_t, c, t, v, r).reasoning
v = f(z_t, c, t, v, r).v_prediction

# Flow matching loss on final v-prediction
loss = flow_matching_loss(v, v_target)
loss.backward()
```
This gives the model multiple "thinking" iterations per denoising step, with gradients flowing through the entire final answer update cycle (both its reasoning steps and the answer pass) for memory efficiency across the Y−1 earlier cycles.
# Initial Experiments
We extend Flux's double-stream transformer (image + text tokens) with a **third reasoning stream** of learned tokens, each with their own QKV projections, layer norms, MLPs, and modulation. All three streams participate in joint multi-head attention. 
# Preliminary Results
Initial experiments (typical config: 5 reasoning steps, 3 answer steps, 512 reasoning tokens) show the reasoning model **outperforms a parameter-matched non-reasoning baseline on Stratified Loss**. The gap between 2.7B with reasoning (size of a 2B model after a DoubleStream→TripleStream change) vs. 2.7B without reasoning (5.8e-3 at 150k steps) is significantly larger (\~6.85x) than the gap between a 2.7B and a 2B non-reasoning model (8.5e-4).
Key observations:
- Improved global structure in generated images
- Benefits are **concentrated in early denoising steps**, consistent with the hypothesis that reasoning helps resolve high-level layout decisions

# Potential Benefits and Outcomes
**Community impact - GPU-poor models**: A small reasoning model may match the quality of a much larger standard model, providing a strong option for users with limited VRAM.
**Distillation path**: Train a large reasoning model (e.g., 32B) that benefits from extended test-time compute, then distill back into fewer steps. This is speculative but could yield a very capable compact model.
**Post-training / RLHF axis**: The reasoning token stream opens a natural path for optimizing information retention across diffusion timesteps using post-training objectives (e.g., GRPO).
**Test-time compute scaling**: Provides an additional axis for test-time scaling in Max-style models, complementing parallel generation + best-of-N selection with depth-based scaling.
**Sister project — Visual reasoning across frames**: A parallel direction applies this unrolling approach across frames generated autoregressively by a multimodal model, where consecutive frames serve as "updated answers." This would be a form of visual-space reasoning for image editing or generation. However, this feels better to explore once we have an autoregressive Flux.3 variant.
# Downsides & Risks
- **Slower training and inference**: The multi-pass forward loop significantly increases compute per training step and per denoising step.
- **Memory intensive during training**: Back-propagating gradients through multiple forward passes can create scaling challenges.
- **Limited API model benefit**: For large API models where we can already run bigger networks, the VRAM vs step trade-off may not be beneficial.
# Compute Needs
- Unrolling multiple steps is VRAM hungry. Even small runs need to be sharded across \~4 nodes on the GB200.
- Minimum viable: 10 Nodes
- Ideal: 24 Nodes
# Open Questions & Next Research Steps
- [ ] Can this reasoning ability be **fine-tuned into a pre-trained model** in post-training (without training from scratch)?
- [ ] Evaluate on downstream metrics: **FID**, **CLIP Score**, human preference evals
- [ ] How does this compare to other test-time compute extensions, such as **more diffusion steps** or **repeated denoising steps **(initial visual comparisons suggest its better, but not finalized)?
- [ ] Can we distill the reasoning model into a standard forward-pass model?
- [ ] Investigate optimal reasoning/answer step ratios (X reasoning steps, Y answer updates)

content: {"metadata":{"type":"page"},"title":"RL Post-Training","url":"https://www.notion.so/316c370222d580ab8761e9ca36fb3f83","text":"Here is the result of "view" for the Page with URL https://www.notion.so/316c370222d580ab8761e9ca36fb3f83 as of 2026-03-17T20:07:48.861Z: {"title":"RL Post-Training"} People currently signed up as core contributors: , , \ - **Research question:** Can RL post-training (specifically GRPO-family methods) yield step-change improvements in compositional accuracy, text rendering, and human preference alignment for Flux3 image and video models? We measure success via large-scale human eval win-rates against the base model conducted via Prolific. - **Expected output artifacts:** paper (method + scaling analysis), open-source RL training framework for flow-matching models (low priority, conditional on novelty, quality of results, etc.), trained reward models, RL-tuned Flux checkpoints with improvements in text rendering, prompt following, visual coherence & consistency, human preference scores. - **Exploration phase:** 2-3 researchers, \~8-16 GB200 nodes for \~2-3 months. **Scale-up phase:** \~50 GB200 nodes for 2-3 weeks. ## Motivation Pre-trained flow-matching models optimize a score-matching loss that approximates the training data distribution. This produces capable generalist models, but as observed across multiple independent studies, the resulting outputs exhibit consistent weaknesses in compositional accuracy, text rendering, and alignment with human preferences \[3,4,5,7,8\]. Zhang et al. \[5\] attribute this to the pre-training distribution itself: quality is dependent on web-scale text-image pairs, and weakly supervised training at this scale is effective for breadth but leaves specific downstream properties unoptimized. Black et al. \[3\] frame the issue more generally—most applications of diffusion models target downstream objectives such as human-perceived quality, not likelihoods, yet the training loss optimizes only the latter. RL post-training addresses this gap by directly optimizing the model's sampling policy against reward functions that score individual outputs \[3,4\]. While RL is less common in diffusion than in LLMs, RL post-training for diffusion models has been rising in popularity. Recent publications from ByteDance, Pinterest/Z-Image, and others substantially de-risk the approach and identify RL as a critical missing step in our current post-training pipeline—one where the methodology is mature and the failure modes are increasingly well-characterized \[14–18\]. At the same time, the number of open-weight reward and preference models has grown significantly in size and scope. From recent literature, the trend appears to be converging on GRPO-style methods with multi-reward objectives, using a fine-tuned VLM trained on human preferences as the reward model. Most recently, GRPO-based methods—borrowing value-free group-relative advantage estimation from DeepSeek-R1 \[2\]—have produced the strongest results to date. Flow-GRPO \[7\] improved SD3.5 Medium from 63% to 95% on GenEval and from 59% to 92% on text rendering. DanceGRPO \[8\] demonstrated a unified framework across diffusion and rectified-flow models, three tasks (T2I, T2V, I2V), four foundation models (including FLUX.1-dev), and five reward models, achieving significant overall benchmark improvements. ## Preliminary Results We implemented Flow-GRPO and Dance-GRPO in schwarzwald (our internal training framework) for Flux2 models and successfully fine-tuned Flux2 T2I models using the following reward functions: OCR, HPSv2, and UnifiedReward. ### 3.2 Reward Hacking & Diversity loss Reward hacking occurs when the model discovers patterns that score highly on the proxy reward but produce visually degraded outputs—oversaturated textures, repetitive background artifacts, mode collapse to narrow "reward-optimal" templates. This is inevitable when using the scores from a reward model as a proxy for human intent without some form of regularization: for any reward function, the unconstrained optimal policy is a delta distribution \[14\]. Recent work \[15\] systematically catalogs these failure modes across multiple reward models and shows that even multi-reward ensembles only partially mitigate the problem. This also aligns with our experience with GRPO on Flux2 (see above image samples). Recent countermeasures developed specifically for diffusion RL: **GARDO** \[16\] introduces adaptive reference-model updates (preventing the reference from going stale) combined with diversity-aware reward amplification for high-quality diverse samples. **GRPO-Guard** \[28\] identifies a root cause of reward hacking specific to flow-matching models: a mean shift and variance disparity in the importance-ratio distribution across noise levels, stemming from the mismatch between Gaussian (diffusion) and discrete (LLM) probability spaces that FlowGRPO inherits from GRPO. **DDRL** \[29\] demonstrates that on-policy regularization—as used by DanceGRPO and FlowGRPO—is itself a source of reward hacking: those methods achieve higher proxy rewards, but human raters consistently prefer the base model's outputs (e.g., DanceGRPO on Cosmos2.5-2B yields –10.5% human preference delta despite higher VideoAlign scores). DDRL addresses this by anchoring to an off-policy data distribution via forward KL divergence, which is equivalent to the standard diffusion training objective and guarantees unbiased RL optimization. **DMDR** \[31\] shows that the distribution matching distillation (DMD) loss is a more effective regularizer for diffusion RL than traditional KL penalties—by performing RL concurrently with distillation rather than sequentially, DMDR enables few-step generators to exceed the quality of their multi-step teachers while maintaining mode coverage. Our plan for Flux3 involves a targeted exploration of the following standard regularization techniques from the literature: adaptive KL with periodic reference updates, multi-reward advantage normalization (as in DanceGRPO), a denoising-loss preservation term that prevents catastrophic forgetting of the base distribution \[5\], and a distribution matching loss. ### 3.3 Sampling Efficiency & Video Extension **Sampling cost.** Online RL requires generating full denoising trajectories (20–50 steps) per training sample. For Flux3-scale models this is 10–30× more expensive than a single gradient step. TreeGRPO \[19\] reduces cost \~2.4× via prefix reuse (branching search trees from shared initial noise). MixGRPO \[20\] proposes mixed ODE-SDE sampling to cut overhead further. Adapting these to Flux3 and finding the optimal compute split between rollout generation and policy updates is a critical engineering problem. **Video.** BFL's video model (SOTA) introduces temporal reward dimensions—motion quality, temporal consistency, physics plausibility—that are poorly captured by frame-level reward models. DanceGRPO \[8\] showed initial success with VideoAlign rewards on HunyuanVideo but found the text-video alignment dimension too unstable for training. Developing temporally-aware reward models that remain stable under RL optimization is an open research problem. ## Reward Model Training The quality of RL post-training is bottlenecked by the reward model. CLIP-based scorers (HPS-v2 \[11\], PickScore) and Bradley-Terry trained models (ImageReward \[12\]) compress human preferences into a single scalar, collapsing dimensions that trade off against each other and creating exploitable surfaces for reward hacking. UnifiedReward \[32\] takes a different approach: it is the first reward model that jointly assesses image generation, video generation, image understanding, and video understanding within a single model. By learning to evaluate across these tasks simultaneously, it exploits synergies—improved image understanding enhances generation assessment, and refined image evaluation benefits video scoring through better frame analysis. UnifiedReward supports both pairwise ranking and pointwise scoring, and its preference data pipeline (pair ranking followed by point sifting) enables automatic construction of high-quality DPO training pairs. We used UnifiedReward as one of our reward signals in the preliminary Flux2 experiments described above. RewardDance \[27\] introduces a generative reward paradigm that fundamentally changes the scaling picture. Rather than training a classifier head on top of a frozen vision encoder, it reformulates reward scoring as a VLM's probability of predicting a "yes" token—indicating that a generated image outperforms a reference image on specified criteria. This formulation intrinsically aligns the reward objective with VLM architectures and unlocks scaling along multiple axes. Our plan builds on these findings. We will (a) train a multi-dimensional generative reward model following the UnifiedReward & RewardDance paradigms, (b) scale the RM to match or exceed 26B parameters, exploiting the demonstrated correlation between RM scale and reward hacking resistance; and (c) incorporate context scaling with chain-of-thought assessment to handle complex compositional prompts. **Video reward models remain a critical gap.** While the image reward model landscape is maturing, video reward modeling is substantially less developed. Evaluating a generated video requires assessing temporal dimensions—motion quality, temporal consistency, physics plausibility, identity persistence across frames—that have no analogue in single-image scoring. These dimensions interact: a video can have high per-frame aesthetic quality but exhibit melting objects or drifting identities across time. VideoAlign \[33\] (Kwai/Kling team, NeurIPS 2025) is currently the only mature open-weight video reward model; it trains a multi-dimensional scorer on top of Qwen2-VL-2B using 182K annotated preference triplets across 12 T2V models, evaluating text alignment, visual quality, and motion quality via separate tokens per dimension. However, as DanceGRPO \[8\] found, the text-video alignment dimension proved too unstable for RL training. Beyond VideoAlign, open-weight options are scarce—most video quality assessment work remains either closed-source or limited to narrow benchmarks. Recent efforts like patch-level reward models (HALO) and frequency-domain temporal consistency metrics are promising but not yet validated as RL training signals at scale. Training our own video reward model—or fine-tuning a VLM backbone with temporal awareness—will likely be necessary for the video extension of this work. ## References \[1\] Ouyang, L. et al. This requires research into what is available and could involve curated task suites, automated success detection, or human evaluation protocols. 3. **Proof-of-concept model.** Train a basic action prediction model on our collected data and evaluate it with our evaluation framework.
