{"metadata":{"type":"page"},"title":"Improved Word-to-Concept Binding for Multi-Reference Image Generation","url":"https://www.notion.so/317c370222d581d8ab46f94c28d831d3","text":"Here is the result of "view" for the Page with URL https://www.notion.so/317c370222d581d8ab46f94c28d831d3 as of 2026-03-02T16:48:34.765Z: {"title":"Improved Word-to-Concept Binding for Multi-Reference Image Generation"} # TL;DR Explore better mechanisms to bind visual reference images to their corresponding subject words in text prompts for multi-reference image generation. Current extended-attention approaches rely on naive attention to infer which reference image maps to which word, which struggles with semantically similar subjects or many references. We propose two directions: (1) positional embedding modifications to explicitly link reference tokens to their paired text words, and (2) visual modulation of text encoder embeddings (e.g., via CLIP features) to inject subject identity at the encoder level, leveraging the LLM's semantic reasoning. # Motivation Single reference flows already work remarkably well, but we still have gaps in multi-subject scenarios where a key challenge is **word-to-concept binding**: the model must learn which reference image corresponds to which subject word in the prompt. Current approaches in Flux supply reference images as **in-context tokens in the MMDiT sequence, **i.e., reference image patch tokens are concatenated directly into the joint text+image token sequence processed by the transformer. This is simple and general, but has a fundamental limitation: the model must learn the binding between reference images and text subjects purely through attention patterns within the shared sequence. This works reasonably well for simple cases (e.g., one or two visually distinct references), but struggles in harder scenarios: - **Semantically similar references**: When two reference images depict similar objects (e.g., two different dogs, or a red car and a blue car), the model sometimes confuses which reference belongs to which text subject, leading to identity blending. - **Many references**: As the number of reference images grows, the model increasingly defaults to an "average" of all references, or to discarding some of them. These failure modes are well-documented in the literature. FastComposer \[1\] identified unrestricted cross-attention as the root cause of identity blending in multi-subject generation. MOSAIC \[2\] showed that multi-subject methods typically degrade beyond 3 subjects. The recent CAG framework \[3\] demonstrated that explicit correspondence-aware masked attention can significantly improve multi-subject fidelity. The core insight across these works is consistent: **implicit binding through attention alone is hard, and explicit structural mechanisms can make the problem easier.** # Core Idea We propose two exploratory approaches to improve word-to-concept binding in our multi-reference architecture: ## Approach 1: Simple Positional Embedding-Based Binding The idea is to use the positional embedding mechanism to explicitly signal which reference image tokens belong to which text word. Since reference images are in-context tokens in the MMDiT sequence, they already receive positional embeddings, but these positions currently encode only the spatial layout of the image and not *what subject it belongs to*. We want to add a binding signal. Two sub-variants we can explore: **1a. Shared Sequence Position (Lightweight)** Assign reference image tokens the same base position on the sequence axis as their paired text word. Since Flux uses RoPE-style encodings, tokens at similar positions naturally attend more strongly to each other. This creates an immediate inductive bias for the model to associate reference tokens with their corresponding text tokens. The challenge: each reference image produces many patch tokens (e.g., 256-1024) that would all share one text token's position. If this is too strong, we may be able to handle this by using the text token position as a base, with small sub-token offsets for each patch: ```python # Pseudocode: Shared sequence position with sub-token offsets # text_pos[subject_word] = p (the word's position in the sequence) # ref_patches = N patch tokens from reference image for this subject for i, patch_token in enumerate(ref_patches): # Base position from paired text word, offset within a small range patch_token.seq_pos = text_pos[subject_word] + (i / N) * epsilon # Spatial position (height, width) remains as normal from the image grid patch_token.spatial_pos = original_spatial_pos(i) ``` **1b. Extra Positional Dimension ("Binding Axis")** Add an extra dimension to the existing positional encoding that acts as a "binding ID." All tokens related to a given subject — the subject's text token(s) and the corresponding reference image tokens — share the same value on this binding axis. Unbound tokens (background text, target image tokens) receive a neutral or default binding ID. ```python # Pseudocode: Binding axis in positional encoding # Standard Flux pos_emb has sequence + spatial components # We add a binding component binding_ids = { "subject_A_text_tokens": 1, "subject_A_ref_patches": 1, "subject_B_text_tokens": 2, "subject_B_ref_patches": 2, "other_tokens": 0, # neutral / unbound } binding_emb = learned_binding_encoder(binding_ids) # -> (dim,) # Option A: Additive (simple, may interfere with spatial info) pos_emb = standard_pos_emb + alpha * binding_emb # Option B: Concatenate to RoPE frequency pairs (cleaner separation) # Add extra frequency pair(s) to the RoPE encoding dedicated to binding rope_freqs = concat(standard_rope_freqs, binding_rope_freqs) ``` This is more expressive than 1a because the binding signal is decoupled from the sequence position, but requires adding parameters (the binding embedding) and modifying the positional encoding dimensionality. ## Approach 2: Visual Modulation of Text Embeddings Instead of relying solely on the DiT to resolve binding, we inject visual information about each reference subject into the corresponding text token embeddings **before** they are processed by the text encoder (LLM/VLM). By modulating the input to the language model rather than its output, we can allow the LLM's own multi-layer attention and reasoning to propagate visual identity information across related tokens in the entire prompt context. **Architecture**: ```javascript Reference Images ──→ [CLIP / SigLIP Encoder] ──→ visual_emb (per subject) │ ▼ Text Prompt ──→ [Tokenizer] ──→ input_embs ──→ [Modulation] ──→ enriched_input_embs │ ▼ [T5 / LLM Encoder] │ ▼ identity-aware text_embs │ ▼ ┌────────────────────┐ │ MMDiT Sequence: │ │ [text_embs] │ │ [ref_img_patches] │ │ [target_noisy] │ └────────────────────┘ ``` **Flux3 / QwenVL — the native path**: With QwenVL as the backbone, this approach becomes architecturally easier. QwenVL already has an image tower that processes images into token sequences that are interleaved with text tokens. We can simply format the input as interleaved image-text, and apply some averaging or learned compacting (e.g., via QFormer) of the image tokens. ```javascript ref_image_A [subject A] and ref_image_B [subject B] are walking together in a park ``` # Potential Benefits and Outcomes - Improved multi-subject fidelity. - Better scalability to many references. - Hopefully generalizable and with minimal modification to current model # Downsides & Risks - **Approach 1** may introduce conflicts between binding positional signals and spatial positional information. It could also be that PEs are not a strong enough mechanism to enforce this information blending. - **Approach 2** learning to modify input embeddings before the LLM requires backpropagation through the LLM which requires a lot of compute. It may also be hard to balance - too strong of a modulation may lead to attention-overfitting or out-of-distribution behaviors. Too weak and the visual identity signal gets washed out. Fine-tuning the LLM (or at minimum, using LoRA adapters) may be necessary to teach it to use the visual modulation. - **Training data requirements**: Both approaches need training data with explicit subject-to-reference annotations, which adds curation complexity. - **Inference overhead**: Approach 2 adds an encoding step per reference image; Approach 1 is nearly free at inference. # Compute Needs - Initial prototyping: 2-4 nodes for small-scale ablations on positional-embedding based variants (might even be possible to see results without fine-tuning). - Main experiments: 8-16 nodes for fine-tuning with multi-reference datasets. More nodes if we want to test how this performs when used in midtraining rather than post-training. - Approach 2 with a big LLM (e.g., Flux3 w/ Qwen3VL32B) may require even more. # References \[1\] Xiao, G. et al. (2023). FastComposer: Tuning-Free Multi-Subject Image Generation with Localized Attention. IJCV 2024. [https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.10431](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.10431)

\[2\] (2025). MOSAIC: Multi-Subject Personalized Generation via Correspondence-Aware Alignment and Disentanglement. [https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.01977](https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.01977)

\[3\] (2025). Hierarchical Concept-to-Appearance Guidance for Multi-Subject Image Generation (CAG). [https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.03448](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.03448) "}

## **Scope**
Explore what is feasible and meaningful for production-level diffusion model training at lower precision. **FP8 is the first priority to tackle** — both FP8 pre-training and quantization-aware training/fine-tuning (QAT) — with the goal of delivering a validated recipe, analysis, and writeup (code/blog post/paper) within 1-2 months. The results serve three purposes: (1) inform **FLUX3 FP8 inference** — understanding which layers and precision choices work best for quantized deployment of the BF16-trained FLUX3 model, (2) enable **FLUX3 FP8 post-training/fine-tuning** — applying the FP8 recipe to later-stage training of FLUX3 where compute savings compound over many runs, and (3) establish a proven recipe for **FLUX3+ model training** in lower precision, reducing time and cost for future generations. FLUX3 BF16 serves as a natural baseline for comparing FP8-trained model quality. Over a longer timeline, the shop's scope broadens to **sub-8-bit precision** (FP4, ternary), moving beyond linear layers and communication to include areas like **lower-bit optimizers and attention computation**.
The central question — spanning all precision levels — is one of *granularity*: which layers to quantize, the bit-width for each model component (linear, attention, optimizer states, communication), and the resulting impact on training throughput and quantized inference speed/quality. A key challenge is resolving the **numerical issues** that arise at lower precision — activation outliers, dynamic range mismatches, and precision-sensitive layers (e.g., attention scores, normalization) that can cause training instability or quality degradation if not handled carefully.
## **Motivation and Impact**
**Direct time and cost reduction for future models.** FP8 training can deliver 20-40% throughput improvement and 30%+ memory reduction over BF16. FLUX3 will train in BF16, but a validated FP8 recipe developed now can be adopted for subsequent models — reducing training time and cost for every model generation after FLUX3. It also benefits FLUX3 fine-tuning and continuation runs.
**Training-inference precision alignment.** FLUX3 will be trained in BF16 but deployed with quantized inference (FP8/FP4). This precision gap degrades quality. An FP8-trained model — or BF16 model with quantization-aware fine-tuning — can close this gap, producing checkpoints that are optimized for quantized inference from the start.
**Compounding gains across the stack.** Lower precision isn't limited to linear layers. FP8 attention (the dominant cost in video diffusion), quantized optimizer states, and FP8 communication for distributed training each contribute independently. Combining them unlocks multiplicative speedups that no single optimization can achieve alone.
## **Approach**
**Phase 1 (Month 1-2): FP8 Training and QAT** — the primary deliverable (code + writeup) covers both FP8 pre-training (training from scratch in FP8) and FP8 quantization-aware training/fine-tuning (QAT on a pre-trained BF16 model).
1. **Layer-granularity analysis.** Profile the model architecture (open-source video model or FLUX3) to map per-layer sensitivity to FP8 quantization (building on ViDiT-Q's four-level variance analysis: channel, token, timestep, CFG). Identify which layers can run fully in FP8 and which need mixed precision.
2. **FP8 training recipe.** Implement hybrid-granularity FP8 training — block-wise quantization for weights, token-wise for activations — with dynamic loss scaling and outlier monitoring (kurtosis tracking). Validate on the open-source video model or FLUX3 architecture at smaller scale; direct comparison against FLUX3 BF16 follows once BF16 training begins.
3. **Training-aware FP8 attention.** Extend FP8 beyond linear layers to the 3D attention mechanism using denoising-step-aware precision allocation, adapting quantization granularity based on the noise schedule.
4. **FP8 QAT on open-source video model.** Apply quantization-aware training (QAT) to an open-source video generation model (e.g., Wan2.2, LTX-2) to validate the recipe independently of FLUX3 and produce publishable results.
5. **Quantized inference validation.** Benchmark FP8-trained and QAT checkpoints under quantized inference (FP8, W4A8) to establish baseline quality; compare against FLUX3 BF16 checkpoints when available.
**Phase 2 (Months 3+): Sub-8-Bit and Beyond Linear Layers**
- FP8 quantized All-to-All communication for distributed training
- Attention-specific quantization + sparsity co-design
- FP4 training exploration (weights and/or activations) using adaptive block scaling
- Low-bit optimizer states (FP8 Adam moments) for additional memory reduction
## **Deliverables and Timeline**
To avoid blocking on FLUX3 BF16 training availability, FP8 training will also be explored and validated on an open-source video generation model (e.g., Wan2.2, LTX-2). This provides an independent validation path and publishable results regardless of FLUX3 timeline. A direct FP8 vs BF16 comparison on FLUX3 is the ideal outcome but is not a dependency for the Phase 1 deliverable.
**Phase 1 deliverables:**
- FP8 layer sensitivity map — per-layer precision requirements for the FLUX3 architecture
- FP8 training/QAT recipe — validated on an open-source video DiT and/or the FLUX3 architecture, with throughput/memory measurements
- Writeup — code, analysis, and recommendations (blog post/paper) ready to inform FLUX3 decisions
- FP8 vs BF16 FLUX3 comparison — direct quality comparison including quantized inference (when FLUX3 BF16 is available)
**Phase 2 deliverables:**
- Sub-8-bit feasibility — FP4 training experiments, quantized optimizers, attention quantization
**Baseline measure of success:** A validated FP8 training/QAT recipe with measured throughput improvement (target: \>20%) and quality analysis, demonstrated on an open-source video generation model and/or the FLUX3 architecture, delivered as a writeup with code ready for FLUX3-scale runs. **Extended success:** FP8 matches FLUX3 BF16 quality (FID/FVD parity) and FP8-trained checkpoints produce better quality under quantized inference.
---
## **Detailed Approach**
### **FP8 Training Schemes and Formats**
There are two FP8 training schemes, both supported on our target hardware (Blackwell GB200). They use 8-bit floating-point data formats but differ fundamentally in how they manage dynamic range:
**Float8 (Hopper SM89+, also supported on Blackwell).** The standard FP8 approach using per-tensor or per-token dynamic scaling factors. It uses two underlying data formats with *precision decoupling*: **E4M3** (4-bit exponent, 3-bit mantissa — higher precision, narrower dynamic range) for forward-pass activations and weights, and **E5M2** (5-bit exponent, 2-bit mantissa — lower precision, wider dynamic range) for backward-pass gradients. The scaling factors are computed dynamically (delayed or just-in-time) to map each tensor's value range into the representable FP8 range. This is what our existing Schwarzwald Float8LinearConverter implements via torchao. A key advantage of Float8 is that it **supports FP8 communication** (e.g., FP8 All-to-All collectives for distributed training), which MXFP8 currently does not.
**MXFP8 (Blackwell SM100+ native).** The OCP Microscaling FP8 format, hardware-native on Blackwell GPUs. Instead of per-tensor scaling, MXFP8 uses *block-level shared exponents* — a single shared scale factor per block of elements (e.g., 32 elements). This provides finer-grained dynamic range adaptation without the overhead of per-element scales. MXFP8 uses the E4M3 data format for both forward and backward passes, relying on the microscaling mechanism to handle dynamic range rather than switching to E5M2 for gradients. This is what our MXLinearConverter implements. **Limitation:** MXFP8 does not currently support 8-bit communication, so distributed training must use higher-precision collectives.
The two schemes are mutually exclusive in our current infrastructure (enforced in DiffusionEngine). Both are relevant for Phase 1 on Blackwell GB200: **MXFP8** for compute (hardware-native GEMMs) and **Float8** for communication (FP8 collectives). Understanding the tradeoffs between them — and potentially combining their strengths — is part of the exploration.
### **Quantization Granularity**
Beyond the choice of FP8 scheme, quantization granularity — at what scale the scaling factor is computed — determines the precision-performance tradeoff:
- **Per-tensor:** single scale per tensor; fastest but highest quantization error
- **Per-token / per-channel:** one scale per row or column; better for activations with large inter-token dynamic range variation
- **Block-wise (e.g., 128 elements):** good balance for weights; subdivides tensors into fixed-size blocks each with their own scale
- **Tile-wise (3D):** appropriate for video attention tensors with spatial-temporal structure
- **Microscaling (MXFP8):** hardware-native block scaling on Blackwell, bridging block-wise and per-element granularity
We will start with the hybrid approach (block-wise weights + token-wise activations) from InfiR2 and refine based on FLUX3-specific sensitivity analysis.
### **Handling Activation Outliers**
A critical challenge for FP8 training is extreme activation outliers in transformer residual streams, which can exceed 1000x the standard activation magnitude. Two complementary strategies:
1. **Outlier suppression regularization** (TWEO): add a lightweight penalty term during training that constrains activation ranges, preventing outlier emergence.
2. **Architectural monitoring** (FOG): track kurtosis of activation distributions as an early warning metric for FP8 instability. If kurtosis spikes, adjust normalization placement or quantization granularity for affected layers.
### **Denoising-Step-Aware Precision**
Diffusion models have a unique property: quantization sensitivity varies across denoising timesteps. Early steps (high noise) are more tolerant of quantization error, while later steps (fine detail) are more sensitive. Following FPSAttention's approach, we will implement timestep-adaptive precision that allocates higher precision to sensitive denoising stages while using aggressive quantization for noise-tolerant stages.
### **FP8 Attention**
Attention is the dominant compute cost in video diffusion transformers. Most FP8 training work quantizes only linear projections, leaving attention in BF16. We will extend FP8 to the dot-product attention itself (Q·K\^T and Attn·V), targeting the 3D spatial-temporal attention patterns in FLUX3. This requires careful handling of softmax precision (kept in higher precision) and tile-wise quantization adapted to the attention block structure.
---
## **Existing Work in Schwarzwald**
Two prior efforts in Schwarzwald provide the infrastructure and empirical foundation for this shop:
### **PR #157: TP + FP8 + Async (Merged, Dec 2024)**
Added FP8 support to the tensor parallelism stack and benchmarked FP8 training with various parallelism strategies on the Flux architecture. Key results:
- **FP8 linear layers integrated** with TP4 and FSDP configurations, benchmarked on Caviar (ablation RVVAE) runs up to 10k steps.
- **Parallelism strategy findings:** FSDP is consistently more performant than TP within a single node. Async TP showed no visible speedup over native TP at our scale (consistent with PyTorch claims that Async TP benefits appear at \>256 GPUs). Recommended strategy: start with FSDP, add TP only for specific layers if OOM, use hybrid FSDP+TP only when necessary.
- **FP8 + TP interaction validated:** FP8 linear layers work correctly under tensor parallelism with no additional numerical issues beyond standard FP8 training.
### **PR #1067: FP8/MXFP8 Quantization Training Support (Open, Feb 2026)**
Refactored and modularized the FP8 infrastructure, adding Blackwell MXFP8 support. This is the direct predecessor to the proposed work:
- **New quantization package** (src/bfl/modules/quantization/) with Float8LinearConverter (torchao Float8 for Hopper SM89+) and MXLinearConverter (torchao MXFP8 prototype for Blackwell SM100+), replacing the monolithic float8.py.
- **Engine integration:** DiffusionEngine and PipeEngine accept float8_config / mxfp8_config (mutually exclusive), with unified post_optimizer_hook() replacing the old sync_float8_amax + precompute_float8_dynamic_scale pattern.
- **Training correctness validated:** Float8 vs BF16 and MXFP8 vs BF16 training steps produce loss within 5% of BF16 on 2-GPU FSDP. MXFP8 convergence test confirms loss does not explode over 5 steps. MXFP8 + selective activation checkpointing produces valid gradients.
- **Activation checkpointing compatibility:** Expanded save list in ac.py with ops critical for MXFP8 (cudnn_attention, flex_attention, inductor_compiled_code).
- **Benchmarking infrastructure:** benchmark_fp8.py for BF16 vs Float8 vs MXFP8 on linear layers and SingleStreamBlock, with optional profiling and activation checkpointing.
- **Remaining work:** Not yet tested on FLUX 2.5 or FLUX 3 full-scale runs. Quantization is currently limited to linear layers — attention, optimizer states, and communication remain in higher precision.
### **How This Accelerates the Proposed Work**
The existing infrastructure means Phase 1 starts from a strong position rather than from scratch:
1. **Linear FP8 is already working** — the quantization package provides tested Float8 and MXFP8 converters integrated with FSDP and activation checkpointing. The shop's focus shifts to *extending* beyond linear layers (attention, optimizer, communication) and *validating* at FLUX3 scale.
2. **Benchmarking tooling exists** — benchmark_fp8.py can be extended to measure the additional components targeted in this shop.
3. **MXFP8 (Blackwell) path is prototyped** — provides an early path to next-generation hardware quantization formats, relevant for the sub-8-bit exploration in Phase 2.
4. **The immediate next step is clear** — PR #1067's open TODOs (test on FLUX 2.5/3) are exactly Phase 1's first milestone, providing a natural continuation of the work.
---
## **Compute Needs**
Three tiers, with decreasing frequency:
- **Minimal daily dev (4 GPUs, persistent interactive sessions):** Code iteration, unit tests, single-node profiling, layer sensitivity sweeps. Always-on development environment.
- **Mid-size runs (16-64 GPUs):** FP8 QAT on open-source video models, multi-node throughput/memory benchmarking, short training runs. Fast scheduling turnaround is critical — these runs should launch with minimal queue wait to keep the dev feedback loop tight.
- **Big runs (128+ GPUs):** FP8 training validation against FLUX3 BF16 at full scale. Used occasionally for milestone validation.
## **Who Might Work On This**
This shop benefits from:
- Experience with FLUX/diffusion transformer training at scale
- Familiarity with NVIDIA Transformer Engine, FP8 formats, and CUDA kernel development
- Understanding of quantization theory (PTQ, QAT, mixed-precision)
- Familiarity with the Schwarzwald training codebase/infrastructure
## **Key References**
References below focus on FP8/FP4 training for linear layers and communication — the scope of Phase 1 and the near-term sub-8-bit roadmap. Lower-bit optimizers and attention computation (Phase 2 longer-term topics) are not included in the list.
- [**FPSAttention**](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.04648) — Training-aware FP8 + sparsity for video diffusion attention
- [**TWEO**](https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.18150) — Outlier suppression for stable FP8 LLM training
- [**FOG**](https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.20524) — Full FP8 GEMM including attention with kurtosis monitoring
- [**InfiR2**](https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.22536) — Open-source FP8 training recipe with hybrid granularity
- [**FP8-LM**](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.18313) — FP8 precision decoupling and optimizer states
- [**ViDiT-Q**](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.02540) — Per-layer sensitivity analysis for video DiT quantization
- [**FP4 All the Way**](https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.19115) — Sub-8-bit training feasibility and format analysis
- [**Four Over Six**](https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.02010) — Adaptive block scaling for NVFP4 on Blackwell
- [**TerDiT**](https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.14854) — Ternary (2-bit) DiT training with architectural modifications
- [**ERNIE 5.0**](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.04705) — Production FP8 multimodal training at trillion scale

## **Core Idea** You are rendering a video with Genie 3: a falling glass on the left drifts out of frame, you render a few more seconds, then turn back. The glass should have shattered, but it has not. In current "world models", the visible canvas *is* the world state. Off-screen dynamics do not exist. When the camera returns, the model hallucinates a fresh history or freezes the scene where it left off. This is not a minor artifact. It is the core failure mode blocking physical plausibility, interactivity, and multi-observer consistency. Most interactive video generators are **view-conditioned continuation models**: the latent "state" is coupled to what is visible, so off-screen content is underconstrained and can be retroactively altered. The problem becomes starker with multiple observers. If two viewpoints are generated without shared underlying state, contradictions are inevitable, even when each view looks locally plausible. A world model that deserves the name should support multiple observers querying the same evolving reality. The likely fix: separate the world from the canvas. Maintain a persistent latent state that evolves whether or not the camera is watching. Render views by querying that state, not by continuing a pixel sequence. This is the memory layer called for in [BFL's research north star](/305c370222d58027a797d9083e34f7e9?pvs=25), which explicitly targets "generative models with persistent memory state and consistent outputs." Self-Flow gives us the image and video backbone. Latent world states are the research path to the persistent memory that connects that backbone to the simulation, generative UI, and automation applications on our roadmap. It is the layer between generation and world modeling. --- ## **Where Do Current Models Stand?** Genie 3 \[1\] does real-time interactive generation, PAN \[2\] demonstrates action-conditioned long-horizon simulation, Solaris \[3\] forces multi-view consistency in game domains, and V-JEPA 2 \[4\] shows that planning from video can emerge at scale. Whether any of these have learned to separate world state from observation internally is unclear. A sufficiently scaled video prediction model sees countless occlusion-reappearance events in training; it could develop off-screen tracking in principle. The question is empirical, and what we lack is the right **evaluation**: turnaround consistency, counterfactual cameras, multi-observer agreement. If an existing model passes these tests, it has canvas-independent state regardless of architecture. An explicit persistent latent, combined with partial-observability training pressure, is a reasonable approach to making this emergence more likely and more measurable. But the evaluation is the litmus test, not the architecture. **Applications along the way:** each phase maps to a tier on BFL's application roadmap. Persistent state on video (Phase 1) enables generative UIs with spatial memory and consistent editing across views. Action-conditioning (Phase 2) opens simulation with controllable rollouts. Agentic simulation (Phase 3) is the automation path: agent and robot training in generated environments. --- ## **What We Would Build** *A canvas-independent world state loop. State, dynamics, and observation should factor cleanly, but as emergent properties of the right training pressure, not as three modules to engineer separately.* ### **Training signal** **Prediction under partial observability, at scale, is sufficient to force persistent world state to emerge.** If a model must predict observations it cannot currently see (held-out frames, future states, off-screen regions), the only way to minimize loss is to maintain an internal state that persists beyond the current view. Self-Flow \[5\] is the starting point: self-supervised flow matching across image, video, and audio on a shared backbone, with temporal consistency that scales with compute. The extension requires one architectural commitment: a persistent latent (e.g., a set of tokens the model reads and writes across temporal chunks --\> perceiver style?). Process video in chunks and apply the self-flow objective within and across them. If something left the frame three chunks ago, the only way to minimize loss when it reappears is to have retained it in the persistent state. The training signal is joint prediction across multiple observations: frames across time in single-view video, but also across viewpoints in multi-view or paired data. Single-view video is the simplest instance and already abundant at internet scale. Multi-view footage, camera metadata, and synthetic turnarounds are richer instances that more directly pressure multi-observer consistency. A stage-wise recipe similar to V-JEPA 2 is likely the right approach: "action-free pre-training on internet-scale video, followed by post-training with a small amount of interaction data" \[4\]. In our case: pre-train persistent state on single-view video, then post-train with multi-view and action-conditioned data. The specific objective (flow matching, masked prediction, AR) is secondary to the structure: multiple partial observations + persistent state + joint prediction loss. The persistent state should be modality-agnostic from the start. Self-Flow already handles image, video, and audio. A video chunk updates the state, an audio segment updates the state, the model can be queried for either. ### **What emerges** The conceptual structure is a learned, nonlinear generalization of a hidden Markov model \[6\]: latent state, transition dynamics, and an observation process, trained end-to-end at scale. Four properties should emerge without being engineered: **Persistent state.** A learned latent maintained across time, queryable beyond the current view. Test: if the model cannot answer off-screen queries, the state has collapsed into a view-conditioned cache. **Belief update.** Unobserved degrees of freedom are uncertain, not gone. Predicting future observations from carried-forward state only works if the model maintains uncertainty about what it has not seen recently. **Dynamics.** The state evolves with actions and time, forced by the training signal of predicting future observations given past actions. PAN \[2\] validates this for action-conditioned simulation. **Multi-observer consistency.** Multiple observers query the same state; coherence follows from the state being canonical, not from views magically agreeing. This is what distinguishes a world model from a view-continuation model. ### **Extension: agentic simulation** Expose the loop as an environment (query, act, step, render). Use agents to surface consistency bugs and demonstrate planning via rollouts. --- ## **Measuring Success** Persistent state directly attacks the **consistency** axis of BFL's core optimization tuple (latency, controllability, quality, consistency). The turnaround test is a concrete operationalization of what "consistency" means for world models. The minimum bar is a turnaround consistency test: entities leave view, time and actions occur, and revisiting from a new viewpoint preserves existence and plausible dynamics. Basic success means an evaluation suite that specifically punishes canvas-entanglement. Objects should persist through occlusion and camera revisits. Different camera trajectories through the same scene should yield compatible inferred state. Multiple simultaneous observers should produce coherent views, with uncertainty appearing only where the scene is genuinely underconstrained. An interactive demo should sustain off-screen consistency beyond the visible window. Extended success adds multimodal state (a single persistent representation updated by video, audio, and text, queryable across modalities), action-conditioned rollouts that remain consistent over long horizons, and agents that reliably use world-model rollouts for planning. --- ## **Project Phases** **Phase 1: Persistent state on video.**
Self-Flow is BFL's internal backbone, already trained at scale. Phase 1 is a finetuning-scale extension: add persistent latent tokens, apply cross-chunk training pressure, and evaluate on turnaround consistency. This is incremental cost on an existing asset, not a new architecture. Single-observer, no actions yet. \~2 researchers. **Phase 2: Multimodal state + actions.**
Add image, audio, text inputs. Action-conditioning. Counterfactual cameras and multi-observer evaluation *(multi-observer could potentially already go into Phase 1)*. **Phase 3: Agentic simulation + scale.**
Expose as environment. Self-improving evaluation via agents. Scale data and model. Each phase produces a clear artifact (demo, benchmark, or paper) before expanding scope. --- ## **References** 1. **Genie 3.** Real-time interactive world model. [deepmind.google/models/genie](https://deepmind.google/models/genie/) 2. **PAN.** Action-conditioned simulation via latent dynamics. [arXiv:2511.09057](https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.09057) 3. **Solaris.** Multi-view consistency pressure. [arXiv:2602.22208](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.22208) 4. **V-JEPA 2.** Video-scale prediction + planning. [arXiv:2506.09985](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.09985) 5. **Self-Flow.** Self-supervised flow matching across modalities. On arxiv soon :bongo_tap: 6. **Hidden Markov model.** [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hidden_Markov_model) "}

{"metadata":{"type":"page"},"title":"Long Context: Perceiver Style","url":"https://www.notion.so/316c370222d580a385ebf50a05f70883","text":"Here is the result of "view" for the Page with URL https://www.notion.so/316c370222d580a385ebf50a05f70883 as of 2026-03-20T17:12:25.024Z: {"title":"Long Context: Perceiver Style"} **Someone help find a better name please.** ## Motivation Consider a video in which a man appears in the opening frames and a woman appears near the end. If the task is to reconstruct the video, we need to preserve the full spatiotemporal detail; no frame can be safely discarded. But if the task is to generate *an image of the man and woman at the beach*, only a sparse subset of frames carries the relevant context; most of the video can be aggressively compressed without loss of task-relevant information. This motivates an architecture that can dynamically control the degree of compression applied to the input; attending to everything when fidelity demands it, and distilling to a compact representation when the task permits. ## The Idea / Architecture ![](https://prod-files-secure.s3.us-west-2.amazonaws.com/d47c9781-7a36-4f60-98ec-c16fd7b286a6/bd07e9c2-a003-4d4a-874c-f45ba6691550/Screenshot_2026-02-28_at_4.22.37_PM.png?X-Amz-Algorithm=AWS4-HMAC-SHA256&X-Amz-Content-Sha256=UNSIGNED-PAYLOAD&X-Amz-Credential=ASIAZI2LB466XOZLZFYF%2F20260419%2Fus-west-2%2Fs3%2Faws4_request&X-Amz-Date=20260419T164305Z&X-Amz-Expires=3600&X-Amz-Security-Token=IQoJb3JpZ2luX2VjED8aCXVzLXdlc3QtMiJGMEQCIHfGxpVuAAlzIwCShZH1BkvpdvrSfzdYTYlkF29UBD7iAiBwl4V0UzJvWPH6yXMzdRnrVnlRiN8nmzq4YGBpU%2BfTmyr%2FAwgIEAAaDDYzNzQyMzE4MzgwNSIMqFRZaZue%2FraDyN0hKtwDt9oCvqXIvd8t6XtAPgIyG6O2cCxMYu2XYhD1sLTFd6zA2YYmx9hiAAnVYrKxNr47JnZnDpRXKecjR8mZ1pdK6xPZrZYuJBllAl27kCbVrkHuvd38%2FZmpdutzhdO5dM2jOP8EFv8I4CaTvlOOtSedkmRkhxg38mPYHz5kCsBoPvE4TPFvk1QFBX00kiAY3lIfNnrh1B649pLh7JpQgeZyQYV%2BTJcLlAkJgTsx4krrx2SjSQylLGqDof6gVUS1sImCKWPtTZaI7k3L8Mj11iq69e8SDIDx%2FzGyfWmEP9SUW%2F%2FdaMc9Xz9gpMwKCQMRjOnGhEj4fi0A81fah3OpUFOAu%2F%2FawwiMJhVPB6wrO9LGjIcy0gaLeoWRom%2FvQPyF76AQeyEXKGtfEPyROuGBlHX1VevXxUEwyMEtgblnK2xA%2FfvKGPElPkBTpV0i%2B2T7owHZgrOW4glT26IxjTHfAZKKajPgeRCr2v3WbgC6eBBX3T6lwzn0EtYi1jBFxONC1rdtdCg27Zoo0pCaUsoVmy63DauD6G1wLxa%2Fz17M5S7O0MzaNmrwsTHTuTAChiA5%2FjW%2BWAdLPWzRmb5DB32Ln%2FAhRX6v%2FUob%2Bpno5kViVhGSEl0u5dmHo9M81c12SEIwvdSTzwY6pgHvBs61HtNsL8i9pTttboPrr%2FpmYnPq9fff8vj0mjJ580E6CudaIrtQi7qkV%2F3BmycqEKj7b6XqFv1CnHFltdC6ZFALVqVmuJ0WFI%2B8rCphLidi%2Fob7yGMmvMSbyZ%2FSDmwwbTqBgFX74MOtePRMNxia%2FjErFp4VqelWHpODOVvtic%2BnW2%2F3xx41shwbAwHdPJnzARgBH44Ed88ZpFtfwcs81x37c47G&X-Amz-Signature=780c7397f41b11f04f28e89c5c43a1ff3eb25d1e3f525d5a6e97c99301ed8c0d&X-Amz-SignedHeaders=host&x-amz-checksum-mode=ENABLED&x-id=GetObject) *Figure 2 of the Perceiver IO paper* The input array is potentially large context and the latent array is learned with variable sequence length N \<\< M. The latent array goes through a large (multimodal) encoder which cross attends to the context. We can then train smaller (per-modality) diffusion models which themselves cross attend to the latent array. We can train the encoder and diffusion decoder(s) end-to-end using diffusion loss. To allow for variable compression of the potentially large context, we can randomly sample N during training. At inference time a user can then choose a “budget” of tokens N they would like to pay for the generation. Note, that all cross attention in the encoder scales as $`O(M*N)`$, and importantly we avoid full $`M^2`$ attention (except for, e.g., the task of copying the input). There is the possibility of meta-learning N from the input / context but I would not focus on this initially. I have been thinking about dynamic compression for a quite a while but couldn’t really come up how to do it with a decoder-only model. Credit here to Mr Podell for giving me the idea to use encoder-decoder models instead. ## Measuring Success - Can we show that it’s possible to use a small number of latents for task that intuitively don’t need much context of a large input (video) - How does this approach compare to the diffusion/teacher forcing line of work when it comes to long video roll-out. The hope is that, for an autoregressive roll-out where diffusion samples are fed back into the encoder, an encoder-decoder model may deal better with error accumulation than a decoder-only model - Can we show that the encoder learns interesting representations. Personally, I don’t care too much about downstream applications of the encoder itself but rather that it makes the generative modeling part efficient. ## Small PoCs ### Diffusion Autoencoder The idea is really to use this for generative modeling but as a first PoC I wanted to train a small autoencoder. I did so on CIFAR-10 varying M uniformly between 4 and 128.
